lines.line: Who here would you trust, and why?
lines.say: Trust, chum? Constance Lowe, easy. She keeps her word, works like two, and she even had the pennies for Sam's pinning pass through her own hand so nobody could say otherwise. Then there's Jory. He won't name a price till he's seen the wood, but whatever he says it's worth, that's what it's worth. And Tom Harrow pays fair for clean pots, every time. Now Ned Pike and his tinker with the handcart? Ha! The river had that box all along.
lines.thought: Funny, I'd trust Constance with my last penny, and she's the one who carried the box in and took the six, which still stings a bit. Right, enough jawing, Bet's loaf and Jory's gate before his saw starts.

lines.line: What would make tomorrow a good day?
lines.say: Tomorrow, chum? Easy as winking. I'm at Jory's gate before his saw is, a loaf from Bet in my belly, and his whole backlog stacked square, bearers first, by noon. Then a fair few pennies in my hand from Jory himself, and somebody walking up Lark Lane and asking, "Who laid that stack so true?" and Jory jerking his thumb at me! Oh, and no carrying anything in under somebody else's arm. What'd make yours a good one?
lines.thought: Truth is, I've missed Jory three mornings running by turning up late or wandering off. If I'm not stood at that gate when he comes out, there's no stack and no name, just Tom's pots again.

lines.line: You said "no carrying anything in under somebody else's arm." What do you mean by that, and how would it sit with you if it happened?
lines.say: Ha! The green box, chum. Constance worked the hook, I held the back end of the pole firm as a rock, and she's the one walked it in under her arm and took Agnes's six pennies. My hook, my pennies on the pinning, and her name on the finding! Stung, it did, I'll not lie. But Constance is straight as a plank, she earned her share, and Agnes did say out loud that Dilly did most for the bridge, so I laughed it off by sundown. Next time, though, I'll be the one carrying the thing in, easy as winking!
lines.thought: It still pinches more than I let on, being the back end of the pole when it was my hook that brought it up. So this stack at Jory's has to be mine, start to finish, with nobody else's hands on the last board.

lines.line: Who here would you trust, and why?
lines.say: Trust, chum? Constance Lowe, first and foremost. She keeps her word, she passed my pennies to Sam plain as day, and she held Jory to his promise when I'd have let it slide. Jory too, mind. He won't name a price before he's seen the wood, but he's never cheated me. Tom Harrow's straight as a plank: scrub his pots proper and the coins ring in your palm, every time. Ned Pike and his tinker with the handcart, though? Ha! I'd not trust that tale with a bent farthing.
lines.thought: Funny, it's the slow, stubborn ones I'd trust, not the quick talkers like me. Still, Constance walked off with the box and the six pennies, and I'm only half over that sting.

lines.line: What would make tomorrow a good day?
lines.say: Tomorrow, chum? Easy as winking! Jory's backlog done square and true with my own hands on it, a few pennies in my palm for it, and somebody walking past that yard saying "Dilly did that one." Throw in a bargain loaf off Bet and Tom's pots for my bed, and I'll call it a grand day. And not a minute of it spent sitting about!
lines.thought: Funny how folk keep asking me about tomorrow when I've not even caught Jory today yet. I'd best stop chattering at the door and get up Lark Lane before his saw starts without me.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
lines.say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, pleased to know you! I blew into Wendleford a few weeks back with a pack and a pocketful of cheer, looking for any odd job going, and the reeve herself'll tell you I did most to get the new bridge up. Can't stop long, mind, I'm due at Jory Crane's yard before his saw's moving, but if you've a job wants doing, what's it pay?
lines.thought: A stranger asking after me by name, that's the bridge talk spreading, and about time too. Still, I'll not miss Jory again for idle chatter, so if they've nothing paying I'm off up Lark Lane with my last penny for Bet's loaf on the way.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: What are you working towards just now?
lines.say: Working towards Jory's backlog, chum! He's a yard full of flood work and he's said he'll want a hand, so I'm off to stack it square, bearers first, and do it slow and proper so folk can point at it and say Dilly did that one. And a penny loaf off Bet on the way, mind, I never go at a job empty. Easy as winking!
lines.thought: Constance carried the box in and the barley went in without me, so this backlog has to be the one with my name on it. I'll not let Hobb or anybody else beat me to Jory's gate this time.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Who here would you trust, and why?
lines.say: Trust? Constance Lowe, chum, top of the list. She keeps her word, blesses everybody and works like two, though she did carry off the reeve's six pennies under my nose, ha! Jory Crane's straight as his planks, he won't name a price before he's seen the wood but he'll never cheat you on it, and Tom Harrow always pays for clean pots, right on the nail. Agnes the reeve said my name out loud before the whole town, so she's square by me too.
lines.thought: Funny, I'd trust Constance with my last penny and still not trust her to leave the credit where it lies. And Ned Pike's tinker story I'd not trust as far as I could throw his stall.

lines.line: What would make tomorrow a good day?
lines.say: Tomorrow? Easy as winking, chum! Jory's backlog stacked square as a church floor, a few pennies in my fist for it, Bet's loaf in my belly, and somebody walking past that yard saying "Dilly did that." Throw in a bargain at Ned Pike's stall come market day and I'll be grinning like a cat in the cream!
lines.thought: Today's not even started and I'm already planning tomorrow, which is daft when Jory's saw might be moving this minute. I'd best stop chattering at strangers and get up Lark Lane before somebody else takes my place at that far end.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: You said Constance keeps her word, though she carried off the reeve's six pennies under your nose: how do you square those two things when you put her at the top of your list?
lines.say: Square it? Easy as winking, chum, she never broke a word to me! She worked the hook and carried the box in, so the reeve's pennies went to her, fair's fair, and I'll laugh about it but I won't call it crooked. Anyway, Agnes said my name before the whole town, and that's worth more than six pennies any day. Now, I'm off to Bet's and Jory's before the saw starts!
lines.thought: It did sting a bit, watching those pennies go into her palm when it was my hook did the fishing. But she's honest as a loaf, and next time I'll make sure it's my hands carrying the thing in.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Describe yourself in a few words.
lines.say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd-jobber, bridge-raiser, and the hook that fished up the reeve's green box, easy as winking! Haul it, mend it, scrub it, you name it, I'll do it. What's it pay, and is it quick? I've Jory's yard waiting on me this morning.
lines.thought: A stranger at the door asking after me by name, so word's getting round that Dilly's the one who gets things done, and about time too. Still, Jory's saw won't wait, so I'll hear them out quick and grab Bet's loaf on the way up the lane.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: How do the people here see you?
lines.say: How do they see me? Ask Agnes, chum, she said it plain before the whole town that Dilly did most to get that bridge up and Wendleford owes me for it! Tom'll tell you I scrub a pot till it shines, slow and proper these days, and Jory lets me hold the far end of his ash. Mind, some'll say I talk faster than I work, but that's just jealousy, easy as winking.
lines.thought: Truth is, Constance carried the box in and took the six pennies, and half the square probably thinks of me as the loud one who turns up after the job's done. I'd best get to Jory's gate before his saw does and give them something to point at.

sc.trait: I do like to be looked at when the work's done right

lines.line: What's left undone?
lines.say: Undone? Plenty, chum! Jory's flood backlog's sitting in his yard waiting on me this very morning, and I mean to stack it square, bearers first, so nobody can say otherwise. Then there's those muddy cobbles by the pump wanting a sweep before market day. What's that pay, I wonder? Oh, and Agnes says the town owes me, so I'd best see what that's worth, easy as winking!
lines.thought: Truth is, the barley and the box both went in under other folks' arms, and I've one penny and an empty belly to show for it. I'll grab Bet's loaf on the way, and this time Jory's backlog is going to have Dilly's name on it.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
lines.say: My last day? Easy as winking, chum! Up to Jory's at first light and stack one pile so square he'd swear it was done with a ruler, then a penny loaf off Bet, then down to the new bridge and stamp across it end to end so everybody sees me do it. Then I'd go and ask Agnes what that town's debt comes to in pennies, and spend the lot on stew for the house at Tom's!
lines.thought: Last day, they say, as if I'd sit still long enough to have one. Still, it stings that it was Constance carried the box and the last span both, and if I did go I'd want one thing left here that's plainly, wholly Dilly's.

sc.trait: Coins burn a hole in my pocket

lines.question: You said some say you talk faster than you work, and that it's just jealousy; is any of that fair, in your own view?

lines.line: You said some say you talk faster than you work, and that it's just jealousy; is any of that fair, in your own view?
lines.say: Fair? Ha! Well... a pinch of it, chum. I botched Tom's pots rushing them, spoilt Sam's hinge at the bellows, and went off after ford stakes on Dob's say-so that nobody was paying for. But slow and proper I've learned now, and the pots shine, so it's more what I *used* to be, easy as winking!
lines.thought: Truth is I've named the job before I've looked at it more times than I can count, and Constance carried that box in while I held the back end. I'll show them this morning at Jory's, bearers square and mouth shut, and then nobody can say it.

lines.line: Describe yourself in a few words.
lines.say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, the one who did most to get the bridge up, ask the reeve! Hauling, mending, scrubbing, holding the far end flat with my mouth shut, easy as winking, and I'm off to Jory's yard this very minute. Got a job going? What's it pay?
lines.thought: A stranger asking after me by name, that's the bridge talk getting round, and about time. Still, Jory's saw won't wait, so whatever they've got, it'd best be quick and pay in hand.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: How do the people here see you?
lines.say: Ha! Depends who you ask, chum! Agnes the reeve said it out loud before everybody, Dilly did most to get the bridge up and the town owes me. Tom reckons I scrub a fine pot when I go slow, and Jory's learning I can hold the far end flat and keep my trap shut. Mind, Widow Mabry probably thinks I'm a fair bean-sheller, and Abel Tash thinks I'm a nuisance, but he sneers at everybody!
lines.thought: Truth is, half of them likely think I'm all mouth, rushing about and botching things till I learnt slow and proper. And it was Constance who carried that box in under her arm, so I'd best get to Jory's and do something they'll point at.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: What's left undone?
lines.say: Undone? Plenty, chum! Jory's backlog for a start, he said come morning and we'd settle it by the job, so I'm off up Lark Lane before his saw's warm. Then there's the town owing me for the bridge, which I've not seen a penny of yet, and those mucky cobbles by the pump want sweeping before market day. Easy as winking, the lot of it. Who's paying for the cobbles, d'you know?
lines.thought: Barley's in and the box is up, and neither one's got my name on it the way the bridge has, so Jory's backlog has to be the one folk point at. I'd best spend my last penny on Bet's loaf first, though, because I always botch it going at a job empty.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
lines.say: Last day? Ha, chum, I'd cram it full! Penny loaf off Bet, then up to Jory's and do one job so square folk point at it and say Dilly did that one, then sweep those cobbles by the pump for whoever'll pay, and I'd take a turn across the new bridge with my nose in the air. And I'd make Agnes cough up what the town owes me before I go. Easy as winking. Why, you know something I don't?
lines.thought: Funny question to ask a body first thing. If I did leave, there'd be nothing in Wendleford with only my name on it, just a hook on Constance's pole and a bridge Agnes says I helped with. So I'd best get that backlog done proper before anyone else does.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said Abel Tash thinks you're a nuisance; what do you think he sees you do that makes him say so?
because: Others' views come mostly as praise with named quotes; criticism waved off (Dilly, Marigold), joked (Hester), hardened into "hard hearts" (Constance).
Concedes only as past.

lines.line: You said Abel Tash thinks you're a nuisance; what do you think he sees you do that makes him say so?
lines.say: Ha! Fair question, chum. First time I met him I was buzzing round the square asking every soul about the reeve's green box, and he'd seen nothing and didn't fancy being asked. I expect he sees me rattling on about what I'll fix before I've looked at it, and dashing off half-done to the next thing, and he's a carter stuck idle by a broken bridge, so a body like me whizzing about must grate on him like a dry axle. Mind, the bridge is up now, so he can thank me with his wheels!
lines.thought: Truth is, I did promise grand and wander off more than once, and it was Constance carried that box in, not me. Maybe Abel's not all sneer. Still, I'll not lose sleep over it, there's Jory's yard waiting and my belly wants Bet's loaf first.

sc.trait: I'll tell you what I'm fixing before I've so much as looked at it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Describe yourself in a few words.
lines.say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd-jobber and fixer of anything going! Easy as winking. Hauling, mending, pots, bellows, you name it, and it was my hook that brought the reeve's green box up, mind, whatever you've heard. Now, what's it you're wanting doing, and what's it pay?
lines.thought: A stranger asking after me by name, maybe Agnes's word about the bridge is getting round, and about time too. Still, Jory's saw will be going any minute, so whatever this is, it'd best be quick and worth a penny.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: How do the people here see you?
lines.say: Ha! Depends who you ask, chum! Agnes the reeve said it plain before the whole town that Dilly did most to get the bridge up and the town owes me for it, and you can't do better than that. Tom reckons I scrub a pot proper now I've learned to go slow, and Jory lets me hold the far end of his ash, mouth shut and all, easy as winking. Some'll say I talk faster than I work, but they've not seen me at the bellows on a good day!
lines.thought: Truth is, half the town likely thinks of Constance when they think of that green box, and the bridge's last span went in under her hands too. I'd best get up to Jory's yard sharpish and do something nobody can carry off under their arm.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: What's left undone?
lines.say: Undone? Plenty, chum! Jory's flood backlog's sitting in his yard waiting on me, and I'm off there this morning to settle it fair, bearers square and mouth shut. Then there's the cobbles by the pump still slick with mud before market day, and the Wheatsheaf's down to its last barrel of cider. I'll fix the lot easy as winking, soon as somebody names me a price!
lines.thought: That barley and that box both went in under other folks' arms, so I want one job done start to finish that's plainly Dilly's. I've a penny for Bet's loaf first, because I always botch it when I go at a job empty.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
lines.say: Last day? Ha, chum, I'd be up at Jory's gate before his saw, and I'd do one job in that yard so square and true that folk point at it after I'm gone and say "Dilly did that one." Then a penny loaf off Bet, a round of goodbyes, Tom's pots for a last stew, and I'd sweep those muddy cobbles by the pump for free, just so market day remembers me. Easy as winking!
lines.thought: Funny, the box and the barley and the bridge all went in under someone else's arm, and the one thing with my name on it is a few words Agnes said aloud. I'd want something I could put my hand on before I go.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said you'd fix the cobbles, the cider and the backlog "soon as somebody names me a price", yet on your last day you'd sweep the cobbles for free; what would you do about them if nobody ever named a price?
because: cobbles ("Who's paying?")

lines.line: You said you'd fix the cobbles, the cider and the backlog "soon as somebody names me a price", yet on your last day you'd sweep the cobbles for free; what would you do about them if nobody ever named a price?
lines.say: Ha, caught me fair, chum! If nobody ever named a price, I'd sweep them anyway, I can't abide standing about, and a broom's a broom whether there's a penny in it or not. Mind, I'd do it slow and proper, right where the carters can see, so come market day they'd know whose work it was. Can't promise the cider, though. I'm no cooper!
lines.thought: It's the name I'm after more than the pennies, truth be told, though the pennies keep me fed and bedded. Still, Jory first this morning, before Hobb gets my backlog, and the cobbles can wait till after.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
lines.say: Yesterday, chum? Up at the Wheatsheaf, morning to Tom and Wat and Hobb, then off up Lark Lane to Jory's yard, and not a soul there, not even a saw going! So I sat on Widow Mabry's step all afternoon shelling beans and hearing about her sister, and watched Hobb pay his week's rent, eight pennies, while Jory never showed. Come evening I scrubbed Tom's pots slow and proper for three pennies and a stew, paid two for a bed, and slept like a log. Easy as winking. Now, who's asking, and is there a job in it?
lines.thought: Funny sort of thing for a stranger to want, my whole day laid out, but if they're looking for a willing pair of hands they've found 'em. Still, I'm not letting them keep me here long, because Jory's yard is mornings, and I'll not miss him a third time.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: Forget something? Me, chum? Well, maybe one thing nags. Jory never did name a price for that backlog, and I can't for the life of me recall if he said morning at dawn or just "morning." There's a promise or two I've flung about and lost track of, too. That's the way of me. But never mind all that! Who are you, and have you got pots, planks or a job that wants doing?
lines.thought: Odd question from a stranger at the door, like they know something I don't. Still, I'll not stand here chewing on it while Jory's saw starts without me, so it's a penny loaf off Bet and straight up Lark Lane.

sc.trait: I promise things grandly and lose track of them just as quick

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
lines.say: Ha! Funny you say that, chum, because yesterday it did just that. I walked up to Jory's gate first thing calling good morning, and next I knew the afternoon wind was blowing down Lark Lane and I was shelling beans with Widow Mabry. Where the middle went I couldn't tell you; I reckon I was busy fretting over Jory. Now, you've asked me three riddles and not one price, so what's this about, and does it pay?
lines.thought: That's a queer question, and a queerer thing that it's true. Still, Jory's yard won't wait on riddles, so I'll not stand here long.

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
lines.say: Sure? Sure as I'm stood here, chum, mostly! The coins tell me the truth of it. If I went to bed with one penny, I've one penny now, and Tom's stew and the bed under the beams back up the rest. When I'm not certain I ask about. Bet hears everything in the square, Widow Mabry watches the whole lane, and Kit's always down by the bridge. Mind, I believe most of what folk tell me, and that's cost me a morning chasing Dob's ford stakes before now! So who's asking, and is there a job in it?
lines.thought: The odd thing is that the big days, the pole and the hook and the green box coming up, sit sharper in me than yesterday does, and yesterday's got that hole in the middle. I'll not fret over it. My one penny says I'm right enough, and Jory's saw won't wait while I stand here.

sc.trait: I'll chat to anyone and believe most of what they tell me

lines.question: You said you walked up to Jory's gate calling good morning, and next you were on Widow Mabry's step in the afternoon wind; what do you remember of leaving the gate and getting to her step?

lines.line: You said you walked up to Jory's gate calling good morning, and next you were on Widow Mabry's step in the afternoon wind; what do you remember of leaving the gate and getting to her step?
lines.say: Leaving the gate? Well, chum, that's the odd bit, I don't rightly have it. I remember my words going out over the empty yard and the shavings lying still, and then it's the afternoon wind with mud and woodsmoke in it and me coming up to her step. I'd only be guessing at what came between, and I won't sell you a guess dressed up as the goods.
lines.thought: That's a whole morning gone missing, and I'm not used to that from myself. I'll ask Widow Mabry if she saw me hanging about the gate, since she watches the whole lane.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
lines.say: Yesterday, chum? Up before the cock, out of Tom's door and up Lark Lane to Jory's yard, only no Jory, not a saw moving! So I sat on Widow Mabry's step shelling beans and heard all about her sister, watched Hobb pay his week's rent, eight pennies, and waited on that carpenter till the light went. Then back here, scrubbed Tom's pots slow and proper for three pennies and a stew, two for a bed, and slept like a log. Why d'you ask? Got a job going, and what's it pay?
lines.thought: Funny sort to come asking after my whole day, but strangers with questions sometimes have work in their pockets. Still, I've one penny and Jory's backlog waiting, so I'll not let this one keep me off his gate for long.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: Remember, chum? Ha! I promise things grand as a lord and lose 'em by dinner, so there's likely a dozen I've dropped down the back of the settle. There was something Dob said about ford stakes, and somebody I swore I'd help that's gone clean out of my head. But I've got the important bits: Jory's yard of a morning, bearers square, mouth shut! Now, are you after a hand with something, and what's it pay?
lines.thought: There's a nag at the back of my head, like I told someone I'd meet them somewhere and never turned up. Hester, maybe, after the box came up? I'll not let a stranger see me fumbling for it.

sc.trait: I promise things grandly and lose track of them just as quick

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
lines.say: Ha! Does it ever, chum! Yesterday I was at Jory's gate first thing, and next I knew the afternoon wind was blowing mud down Lark Lane and I'd a lapful of bean pods. That's what comes of sitting still: the day slips off when you're not looking. Now, you've asked three questions and named no price, so is there work in this or are you just a curious sort?
lines.thought: Odd thing to ask, and odder that it's true, because I can't for the life of me say where that morning went. This one's either a nosy parker or a wise woman's apprentice, and neither pays, so I'd best get my loaf and get up to Jory's before I lose another morning.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
lines.say: Sure as I'm standing here, chum, mostly! The things I've got coin for, I know cold. Three pennies off Tom last night, two on the bar for the bed, one left in my purse. And there's my hook on my shoulder, so I didn't dream Sam's smithy. The rest I check the easy way: ask Bet over a loaf, ask Widow Mabry, ask whoever was there, and if two of 'em say the same, that's good enough for Dilly. Now, a penny says you've a job behind all these questions, so what's it pay?
lines.thought: Funny sort, asking how I know what I know, like a priest or a reeve's clerk. I'd swear to the pennies and the hook, but that Dob business with the stakes still nags at me, so I'll ask Bet about it after Jory's.

lines.line: You said you waited on the carpenter till the light went, and also that you were at Jory's gate and then the afternoon wind was blowing with bean pods in your lap; how do the gate, the step and the waiting fit together in your day?
lines.say: Easy, chum, it fits like a peg in a hole! First thing I was at Jory's gate, hollering at an empty yard. Then there's a stretch I can't rightly account for, likely kicking my heels up and down the lane. By afternoon I'd settled on the widow's step with the beans, and I stayed there till evening drew in and my belly sent me off to Tom's. "Till the light went" was me stretching it a touch, I'll own that, since I was in the scullery before full dark.
lines.thought: Funny, I truly can't say where that middle of the day went, and I don't much like a hole like that in my own story. This one's sharp, though, and still hasn't named a price.
