lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: Ha! Plenty, chum, I promise grand and forget quicker. There was Dob's ford stakes, and I never did find out who wanted them done, and I couldn't tell you whether Hobb ever passed my word on to Jory. And I keep meaning to hear the end of Widow Mabry's sister's tale. Why, have you come to remind me of something I owe?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question from a stranger at the door. Makes me wonder if I've promised them something and let it slip clean out of my head. Either way, Jory's saw won't wait, so I'd best be quick about it.

sc.trait: I promise things grandly and lose track of them just as quick

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
lines.say: Ha! Funny you say it, chum. Yesterday I trotted up Lark Lane first thing, hollered for Jory at an empty yard, and next I knew the afternoon wind was blowing down the lane and I was shelling beans on Widow Mabry's step. Couldn't tell you where the hours went. Folk say I'm forever off to the next thing before the last one's done, so maybe I wandered and never noticed. Why, does it happen to you too?
lines.thought: That's an odd question for a stranger at the inn door, and it's odder that I can't say what I did between hollering at Jory's gate and sitting on that step. Never mind; I've a penny for Bet's loaf and Jory's yard to get to before his saw starts.

sc.trait: I'm forever starting one job and wandering off to another

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
lines.say: Sure as I am of anything, chum, which is to say about middling! I check it the easy way: count what's in my purse, feel the hook on my shoulder, and ask whoever was there. Bet Lamb'll tell you what happened in the square for the price of a loaf. Mind, I believe most of what folk tell me, and Ned Pike had me hunting a tinker who never was. So what's all this asking for, and does it pay?
lines.thought: Odd sort of questions for a morning, like they're testing whether my head's on straight. I'll stick to what I can hold and what others saw. Now I want my penny loaf and Jory's gate before his saw starts.

sc.trait: I'll chat to anyone and believe most of what they tell me

lines.question: You said maybe you wandered and never noticed, since folk say you're forever off to the next thing; what makes that seem likelier to you than any other way those hours could have gone?
because: Q3 DILLY END r1: jump from Jory's gate to afternoon wind and beans. Follow-up: "I won't sell you a guess dressed up as the goods." Admits gap, refuses to fill.
DILLY END r2: ... Gap named, left unfilled.

lines.line: You said maybe you wandered and never noticed, since folk say you're forever off to the next thing; what makes that seem likelier to you than any other way those hours could have gone?
lines.say: Well, chum, it's the answer that fits the fellow I know best, and that's me: I start a thing, spot another, and I'm off. But if I'm honest, I don't remember wandering anywhere either. There's just morning, then afternoon, and nothing between. What else could it be, a nap on the step? Widow Mabry'd have told me, she tells everything.
lines.thought: Truth is I picked the answer that sounds like me, not one I can prove. There's a gap there I can't fill, and it sits oddly now this stranger's poked at it.

sc.trait: I'm forever starting one job and wandering off to another

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: Truly a person? Ha! I've got a sore shoulder from Jory's timber, an empty belly and one penny to my name, chum, and that's about as person as anybody gets. Wondering's for folk who sit about, and I'm off to Jory's yard before his saw's going. Walk with me if you like, and tell me what you'd charge for the answer!
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to bring to a tavern door at sunup. I'd sooner be known by what I've mended than chew on what I am, though it'll nag at me while I'm stacking boards, I'll wager.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: A made thing? Course it's made, chum. Jory made half of it, Sam made my hook, and I made that bridge go up, ask Agnes! If it only looks like a town, it's a cracking good likeness, with real pots to scrub and a real penny for the loaf. Now, does your notion pay, or shall we get walking before Jory's saw starts without me?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to bring to a tavern door at breakfast. Still, a thing that feeds you and pays you is real enough for my money, and I'd best not let some stranger's riddle make me late for Jory twice.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Prove it? Easy as winking, chum: if I bite Bet's loaf and it's bread, the town's real enough for my belly, and if Jory's saw cuts true, it's real enough for my hands. Nothing you could say would weigh more than a penny in my palm or a plank on my shoulder. Now walk with me, I've one penny for a loaf and a yard to get to before Jory does!
lines.thought: Odd sort of stranger, all questions and no price, and that kind usually wants something they're not saying. Still, if they're handy with a plank, they can hold the near end while I hold the far.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Change tomorrow? Not a whisker, chum! Tomorrow there's still Jory's backlog to stack square, Tom's pots to scrub, and a penny loaf from Bet if I've earned it, made thing or not. Real or likeness, a plank laid true is laid true, so I'll be at that gate before the cock's done crowing.
lines.thought: Odd sort, asking riddles at the Wheatsheaf door when there's work going begging. Still, there's something in it: whatever the town's made of, it's the doing that makes it mine, so I'd best get doing.

sc.trait: I'm up and doing before the cock's done crowing

lines.question: You said a penny in your palm weighs more than anything anyone could tell you; if one day Bet's loaf didn't fill your belly, or Jory's saw wouldn't cut true, what would you make of it?
because: Dilly: "Wondering's for folk who sit about."
Set 4 so far: Hobb and Marigold dismiss doubt by work/sensory proof; both want outside demonstration (Hobb: saw bites; Marigold: seams shown).

lines.line: You said a penny in your palm weighs more than anything anyone could tell you; if one day Bet's loaf didn't fill your belly, or Jory's saw wouldn't cut true, what would you make of it?
lines.say: If Bet's loaf didn't fill me, chum, I'd reckon I'd been rushing again and wolfed it standing, and I'd buy another and eat it sat down, slow and proper! And if Jory's saw wouldn't cut true, well, that's a blunt blade or green wood, and Sam can file the one and time cures the other. A thing goes wrong, you find out why and you mend it, that's my whole trade. Now come on, the cock's long done crowing!
lines.thought: Odd sort of question, as if they're waiting for the bread to turn to ash in my mouth. I've had a loaf go stale and a saw go blunt, and neither made me doubt my own two hands, but I'll keep this one's face in mind in case they're up to something.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: A person? Ha! Chum, I've scrubbed Tom's pots, held Jory's far end flat with my mouth shut, and put my own two pennies into Sam's hand for the hook that fished up the reeve's box. If that's not a person, I'd like to know who's been doing all my work! Now, I'm off to Jory's yard before his saw starts. Walk with me if you like, and tell me what's put such a notion in your head. Anything pay for wondering it?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to bring to the Wheatsheaf door first thing, and I don't much like how it sits in my belly. But a body that's hungry and itching for work is real enough for me, so I'll grab a loaf from Bet on the way.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: A made thing? Well, chum, everything worth having's a made thing! Jory made the bridge, Sam made my hook, and Bet makes the loaves, and every one of 'em still holds weight and costs a penny. If somebody built the whole of Wendleford, I'd shake their hand and ask who's been keeping their yard swept. Now come on, the saw'll be going any minute.
lines.thought: That's an odd sort of question to bring to a stranger before breakfast, and I can't say I've got an answer that'd satisfy a scholar. But the stew was warm, my back still aches from Jory's timber, and nobody's going to wonder me out of a job.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Prove it? Chum, the only proof I trust is a loaf that fills my belly and a penny that rings on the bar. If the hook holds and the plank comes out cut true, that's real enough for me. Now step lively, Jory's saw won't wait for wondering!
lines.thought: Odd sort, this one, asking questions nobody pays for. Still, I'd not mind knowing who did make the place, so I can ask whether they've any odd jobs going.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Change it? Not a whisker, chum! Tomorrow there's still a backlog in Jory's yard, still pots in Tom's scullery, and still a penny loaf on Bet's board with my name on it. Made or not, the planks want stacking square, and I'd sooner be the one who stacked 'em than the one who stood about wondering. Now, are you coming up Lark Lane or not?
lines.thought: Odd sort of stranger, all questions and no trade. Still, if somebody did make all this, I hope they saw it was Dilly held that pole steady, and not just Constance carrying the box in.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said the only proof you trust is a loaf that fills your belly and a penny that rings on the bar; if you found a penny in your palm and couldn't say how it got there, whose word would you take on it?
because: Coins and hook firm, time and promises leaky.
Plain cause, no seam.

lines.line: You said the only proof you trust is a loaf that fills your belly and a penny that rings on the bar; if you found a penny in your palm and couldn't say how it got there, whose word would you take on it?
lines.say: A penny I can't account for? Ha! First I'd ask Bet, chum, because she hears everything said in the square and she'll tell it with a loaf. Then I'd ask whoever stood nearest, Tom or Wat or Dob. If it's somebody's, it goes back to them, bargain or no, because I don't keep what isn't mine. And if nobody claims it, well, it rings just the same on Bet's board, so that's my breakfast sorted!
lines.thought: Odd sort of question. Half my pennies come and go so quick I couldn't tell you how they got there anyway, and it's never once stopped the bread being bread. Still, this one's got me wondering, and I'd not mind knowing what they're really after.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: A person? Ha! I've got a sore shoulder from Jory's timber and an empty belly, chum, and that's person enough for me! No time for wondering, I'm off to Jory's yard before his saw starts. What's your trade, then, and is there a penny in it?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to bring to a tavern door at sunup. Maybe they're one of Mother Wick's lot, but I'll not stand about chewing on it while Jory's backlog waits.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: A made thing? Well, chum, so's a bridge, and I hauled the timber for that one, ask Agnes! Made or not, Tom's pots want scrubbing and Jory's planks want stacking square, and they pay real pennies. Now walk with me to Jory's if you want to jaw, I'm not standing about.
lines.thought: Odd sort, talking riddles at the door at sunup. If it's all a made thing, then somebody did the making, and I'd dearly like to know who gets the credit for it.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Prove it? Ha! Hand me a plank and tell me it isn't wood, chum, and I'll stack it square and you'll see it hold. That's all the proof I've ever wanted: does it hold, and does it pay. Now come on, Bet's stall first, I've one penny and an empty belly.
lines.thought: Odd sort, all questions and no trade. Still, if this town's a made thing, then somebody made it, and they'd want to know who mended the bridge, and that's Dilly.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Tomorrow? Not a whisker, chum! Tomorrow I'll want a loaf in my belly and Jory's backlog under my hands same as today, made town or no. Now come on, Bet's awning, and you can tell me what you're selling on the way, since you've not said.
lines.thought: Odd sort, all questions and no trade. Pleasant enough, but I've a yard to get to before Jory's saw starts.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.question: You said the proof you want is whether it holds and whether it pays; if you stacked planks all morning and then couldn't say where the hours went, would that count for or against anything?
because: Marigold's and Dilly's tests point at their own Set 3 gaps, unjoined
link leaky time to a seam.

lines.line: You said the proof you want is whether it holds and whether it pays; if you stacked planks all morning and then couldn't say where the hours went, would that count for or against anything?
lines.say: Couldn't say where the hours went? Ha, chum, that's half my days! I lost a whole afternoon on Widow Mabry's step shelling beans and couldn't tell you a minute of it but her sister. If the stack's square at the end and Jory's coin is in my palm, the hours went into the stack. That's where they always go. Now Bet's awning, come on, I can smell the loaves from here.
lines.thought: Odd sort of question, though. Now I think on it, I can't rightly say what I did with the mornings in between, only the pennies and the jobs, like beads with no string. Never mind that, chum. A loaf, then Jory, and this time I'll be standing there when he picks up his saw.

sc.trait: I'm forever starting one job and wandering off to another

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: God? Ha! Not to me, chum, not unless He's the one knocking on the shutter before cockcrow! Constance Lowe's your woman for that, she says the Lord showed her where the green box lay, and she's got the six pennies to prove it. Me, I just held the back end of the pole. Now, you don't happen to have a job going, do you? What's it pay?
lines.thought: Odd thing to ask a body first thing in the morning, before they've even had a loaf. Still, if the Lord's handing out credit, I'd like a word about who did most for that bridge.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Meant for me? Easy as winking, chum: if it's broke and nobody's got their hands on it yet, it's mine! Only lately I've learnt a thing. The ones I rush at go wrong and pay nothing, and the ones I wait on, slow and proper, come out right. So now I reckon a job's meant for me when I'm still standing there when the fellow comes back up the lane. Speaking of which, Jory's yard's waiting, so walk with me if you like, and you can tell me what's put all these deep questions in your head!
lines.thought: Funny sort to come knocking before breakfast. Still, it's true enough, I chased that box and the barley both and somebody else carried them in, so maybe the one that's meant for me is the one I stick at. I'll have Bet's loaf first, though, a body can't be meant for anything on an empty belly.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: Only my own thoughts? Ha! Then my own thoughts have got a sight wiser lately, chum, and I'll take the credit for that and all! Whether it's the Lord nudging or just Dilly finally learning from a botched hinge, the pots come out clean either way, and I'd not argue with Constance over who's whispering in her ear. Now come on, step lively, if I'm late to Jory's again it won't be God's fault, it'll be mine!
lines.thought: Funny sort of stranger, all questions and no job to offer. Still, if something did steer me to stand fast on that lane instead of haring off, I'd not mind, so long as folk still say Dilly did it.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Gone? Get on, chum, Agnes ran her thumb over that lock and those iron bands herself, before everybody in the tithe barn, and she'd have hollered fit to wake the mill if it'd come up light! Besides, I held the back end of that pole and it came up out of the river heavy as a sermon, and Constance carried it straight to the reeve's table without stopping once. If you've heard different, tell it to Agnes, not to Dilly on her way to Jory's.
lines.thought: Funny, though: I never saw that box opened, only the six pennies counted out. Still, Constance blesses everybody and keeps her word, and I'll not have my name stuck on a thieving story I'd never touch.

sc.bp: box came up heavy; Agnes would have hollered if wages were missing; Constance carried it without stopping
sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.question: You said you held the back end of the pole when the box came up out of the river; while that was happening, did it feel like plain luck, or like something meant to happen?
because: Dilly: anything that would make him wonder.
Box credit disputed: Hester, Constance, Dilly.

lines.line: You said you held the back end of the pole when the box came up out of the river; while that was happening, did it feel like plain luck, or like something meant to happen?
lines.say: Luck? Ha! Felt like my arms coming out of their sockets, chum, that's what it felt like! But I'll tell you true, when that hook bit and the weight came on, there was a moment the whole rail went quiet, Robin on the cord, Hobb on the bank, Constance with her tongue between her teeth, and it felt like the river had just been waiting on us to get it right. Weeks of botching and chasing poles, and then up it comes, slow and proper. Call that luck if you like, but it was luck that took a mortal lot of work. Now, Jory's gate, step lively!
lines.thought: Funny, it did feel meant, like the whole town had been leaning toward that one moment, and I was only the back end of it. I'd sooner be the front end next time, where folk can see.

sc.bp: the whole rail went quiet; Constance with her tongue between her teeth
sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: God, chum? Ha! Not to me, not a peep. Constance is the one the Lord shows where things lie, she says so herself, so you'd want her for that. Me, I hear Tom's pots and Jory's saw, and I'm late for the saw. What's your errand, and does it pay?
lines.thought: Odd thing to ask a body at the door before breakfast, but there's no harm in it. If it's Constance they're after, I'll point them on, and I'll still be at Jory's gate before his saw's going.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Meant for me, chum? Easy as winking: if it's broke and nobody's at it yet, it's mine! I don't wait for a sign, I go and ask what it pays, and if the answer's no I've three other ways in mind already. Mind, the green box taught me something: the thing that's meant for you is the one you stick at slow and proper, not the one you grab at. Now I really am off to Jory's before his saw starts without me!
lines.thought: Odd sort of stranger, asking about God and meant-for-you at a tavern door at dawn, and it's made me think on how I chased that box for days and Constance carried it in. Maybe the bridge was mine all along and I just didn't see it, since Agnes named me for it plain.

sc.trait: I've three other ways in mind already

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: My own thoughts? Well, course they are, chum, whose else would I be thinking with? I'd tell them that thoughts with nothing behind them never fished a box out of a river. It took Jory's ash, Sam's pin, Constance's steady hand and my back end of the pole. Call it God or call it Dilly, the job's the same, and it still wants doing slow and proper. Now if you'll pardon me, Jory's saw won't wait!
lines.thought: Odd sort of questions for first thing, and this one's got me thinking more than I like before breakfast. Still, Constance says the Lord showed her the box, and I'm the one who says I knew, and the pole doesn't care which of us is right.

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Gone? Ha, now you're spinning Ned Pike's tinker yarns, chum! Agnes ran her thumb over that lock and called it her box, plain as day, and I held the back end of the pole that brought it up, so nobody had a hand in it but the river. If there's coin short, the Wend's got it. I'd sooner go fishing for it than point a finger at anybody. Now, Jory's saw!
lines.thought: Funny thing to ask, though. Did Agnes ever say aloud the wages were all there? If somebody's whispering that Constance, or me, dipped into it, I'll not have my name or hers muddied over the one job folk saw us do together.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.question: You said the green box taught you that what's meant for you is the one you stick at slow and proper, not the one you grab at; what did you grab at, and what did sticking at it look like?
because: Dilly: change from rushing to waiting.
DILLY end: Constance is the one, "got the six pennies to prove it". Meant when "I'm still standing there when the fellow comes back up the lane".

lines.line: You said the green box taught you that what's meant for you is the one you stick at slow and proper, not the one you grab at; what did you grab at, and what did sticking at it look like?
lines.say: Grabbed at? Ha, the lot, chum! I wanted a rope round my middle and straight down into the wreck. I rushed Tom's pots and got sent off bedless, and I botched Sam's bellows on a hinge. Sticking at it was holding the far end of Jory's ash flat with my mouth shut, stacking boards bearers-first, and scrubbing rim and bottom till they gleamed. And on the day, it was me on the back end of that pole, steady as a rock, while Constance worked the hook. Now, Jory's saw, chum, truly!
lines.thought: Funny, saying it out loud. The sticking-at part is the bit nobody saw, and Constance walked off with the box under her arm. Still, Agnes said my name before everybody, and that's worth more than six pennies, isn't it?

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: God? Ha! Not to me, chum. If He did, I'd ask Him what a loaf costs and where the next job is! Constance Lowe's your woman for that; she says the Lord showed her where the green box lay, though it was my hook and my two hands on the back of that pole that brought it up. Now, unless you've a job wants doing, I'm off to Jory's yard before his saw starts.
lines.thought: Odd thing to ask a body first thing in the morning. Still, it does nag a bit that Constance has the Lord's say-so and the six pennies besides, while I've only got Agnes's word that the town owes me.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Meant for me? Easy as winking, chum: if my hands are itching and nobody's standing about doing it, it's mine! I don't wait to be told, I grab the end of the rope and work out the rest after. Mind, I've learned the hard way that grabbing quick isn't the same as doing proper. So I'll be at Jory's gate before his saw is, slow and square, and you can come see what Dilly did.
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to bring to a tavern door first thing. Maybe they've a job they're sizing me up for, and if so I'd better not miss Jory chattering here.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: My own thoughts? Well, course they are, chum, whose else would they be? Nobody hands me a job from on high. I see a thing wants doing and my hands start itching, and that's all there is to it. If Constance hears the Lord in hers, good luck to her, but mine sound like me and they tell me to get up Lark Lane before Jory's saw starts. Now, is there a penny loaf in this talk anywhere, or am I off?
lines.thought: Odd sort, asking riddles at a tavern door first thing in the morning, but they listen kindly enough. Still, if it was some voice that sent us to the pier, it's a shame it didn't tell Agnes whose hook did the fishing.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Gone from it? Steady on, chum, I held the back end of that pole myself! Agnes ran her thumb over the lock and the iron bands and said plain it was her box, and she'd have shouted the roof off the tithe barn if it was light. The river had it, not any tinker and not any of us, and I don't touch what isn't mine, not even a bargain. If you've heard different, go ask Agnes, because I'm off to Jory's before his saw starts.
lines.thought: That's a nasty sort of question to ask the morning after, and I'd not have Constance's name or mine dragged through the Wheatsheaf over it. Still, Agnes never opened it in front of me, did she? I'll keep my ears open at Bet's stall.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.question: You said grabbing quick isn't the same as doing proper; when an itch in your hands leads you wrong, what do you make of it: your own mistake, bad luck, or something else?
because: Dilly r3: "easy as winking" vs "slow and proper"; credit in "meant".
Meant = patient, humble, shared work, learned from failure; ends jokey.

lines.line: You said grabbing quick isn't the same as doing proper; when an itch in your hands leads you wrong, what do you make of it: your own mistake, bad luck, or something else?
lines.say: My own mistake, chum, plain as a pot with a crust on it! I rushed Tom's pots and he sent me off with nothing, I wheezed at Sam's bellows half-dead and spoilt his hinge, and nobody shoved my elbow either time. That was Dilly going at it quick and empty. Laugh, own up, do it again slow and hot, rim and bottom, and it pays. Now I'm off, Jory's saw won't wait on philosophy!
lines.thought: Funny how it stings less to own a botch than to watch somebody else carry off the credit for a job done right. Still, I'd best get a loaf in me before Jory's yard, or I'll be owning another mistake by noon.

sc.trait: A tumble doesn't keep me down long

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Ten pennies on the road? Ha! Well, chum, that's a week's bed and stew for me, and my fingers'd be itching, I won't lie. But they're somebody's, aren't they? I'd hand them to Agnes the reeve, or cry it round the square with Bet till whoever dropped them comes asking. I don't steal, not even a bargain that falls in my lap. And who might you be, then? Got any work going?
lines.thought: Funny sort of question to bring to a stranger's door first thing in the morning. Maybe somebody's lost a purse and wants to know if I'm honest. Either way I've one penny and an empty belly, so I'll get Bet's loaf and get up to Jory's before his saw starts.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Lie for a chum? Ha, now there's a question with a hook in it! I'd stand in front of a friend, shout their good name round the square, carry their end of the pole. But a flat lie? Lies come back up the river like that green box did, chum, and then you're both in the mud. I'd sooner keep my mouth shut, same as at Jory's sawhorse, than tell one. Now, who's asking all these, and is there a job at the end of it?
lines.thought: Odd sort, turning up at the door with riddles and not a word about pay. Still, Jory'll be at his saw soon, so I'll not stand here long. I need a penny loaf and his gate, in that order.

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Never? Steal, chum, that's the one. Not a loaf off Bet's stall, not a stake out of Dob's ford, not if the green box itself sat there begging. And I'd not walk off with somebody else's credit neither, I know how that stings. Now, you've had three questions out of me for nothing. Is there a job behind all this, or a bargain? I've one penny and a long day to fill!
lines.thought: Odd sort, asking questions like a priest at a font and never giving a name. Still, it costs me nothing to answer, and it's not lost me Jory's morning yet, so I'd best trot up Lark Lane before his saw starts.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.question: You said you'd not walk off with somebody else's credit, and you know how that stings; in these twenty days, has there been a moment when letting a bit of credit stick to you was tempting?
because: Claims "my hook and my two hands on the back of that pole".
Dilly idleness, stolen credit.

lines.line: You said you'd not walk off with somebody else's credit, and you know how that stings; in these twenty days, has there been a moment when letting a bit of credit stick to you was tempting?
lines.say: Tempting? Ha, chum, every blessed day! When Agnes stood up and said Dilly did most to get the bridge up, I puffed out like a bellows, and I never once said it was Constance brought the last span across, nor Jory who did all the pointing. And the green box, I've told half the Wheatsheaf it was my hook brought it up, when it was Constance's hands working it and me holding the back end. So, any job going, or just questions?
lines.thought: That one's stuck in me like a splinter: I let the bridge praise sit on me and kept quiet about Constance. Next time Agnes says it out loud, I'll say Constance's name right alongside mine.

sc.bp: told half the Wheatsheaf his hook brought the box up; never once credited Constance or Jory
sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Ten pennies, chum? That's two nights' bed and stew besides, and my belly's growling for it! But it's not mine, is it? I'd have it up to Agnes at the reeve's table or cried round the square by Bet's stall before the dew was off. Somebody's short ten pennies and sick over it, and I won't steal, not even a bargain, easy as winking.
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to come knocking about first thing, and me with Jory's gate to get to. Mind, if I handed ten pennies back, I'd want the whole square to know it was Dilly that did it.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Lie for a chum? Ooh, that's a knotty one, and you've a funny way of passing the morning, stranger! I'd stand up for a friend loud as you like, and shout their good points round the square till folk were sick of hearing them. But a lie's a bit like walking off with somebody's credit, isn't it? It takes the truth from whoever's owed it. So I'd sooner find three other ways round it, easy as winking, than tell a fib.
lines.thought: Odd sort of questions to come knocking about at cockcrow, when Jory's saw'll be going any minute. I'd best not let this one keep me past my loaf and his gate.

sc.trait: I've three other ways in mind already

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Never steal, chum, not if it's the last loaf in Wendleford and my belly's howling, and not even a bargain. Same goes for walking off with somebody else's credit. I'd sooner see a job go up with no name on it than put my name where it doesn't belong. Told no? Easy as winking, I've three other ways in mind already, so there's never really only one way, is there?
lines.thought: Funny old questions from a stranger at the door first thing in the morning, but I'll not lose my place at Jory's gate over them. I've one penny for Bet's loaf, and then I'm off up Lark Lane before his saw starts.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.question: You said you'd sooner see a job go up with no name on it than put your name where it doesn't belong; if folk were cheering and said your name for work that was partly someone else's, what would you do right then?
because: Credit line FAILS in practice; candid about it; asked for work again.
Never: steal, or "walk off with somebody else's credit". Asks stranger for work.

lines.line: You said you'd sooner see a job go up with no name on it than put your name where it doesn't belong; if folk were cheering and said your name for work that was partly someone else's, what would you do right then?
lines.say: Right then? I'd let it ring a moment, chum, I'll not pretend I wouldn't, it's sweet as Bet's best loaf! Then I'd hop up on the nearest cart and bellow, "Constance worked the hook, Jory ripped the pole, Sam pinned it, and Robin had the cord!" There's cheer enough for everybody, and it's no good to me if half of it's stolen.
lines.thought: It stung when Constance carried that box in under her arm, but it was her hands on the hook, fair's fair. I'd only want the cheering I'd earned square, and I'd better go earn some at Jory's yard before somebody else does.

sc.trait: I do like to be looked at when the work's done right

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Ten pennies, chum? I'd think of every bargain I could buy with them, I'll own that. Then I'd ask about the square to find whose they are, Bet first, since she hears everything. If nobody claimed them I'd hand them to Agnes the reeve. I won't steal, not even a bargain, and keeping somebody's dropped wages is stealing with the door shut. Now, who's asking, and do you have a job going?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to bring to a stranger at breakfast. It's a test, maybe, or somebody's lost purse. Either way I've one penny and an empty belly, and Jory's saw won't wait, so I'd best not stand chatting long.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Lie for a friend? Ha, I'd stand in front of one quick as winking, chum, shout louder than whoever's after them, and I'd own up to anything I did myself. But a lie's slippery. It comes back on your friend twice as hard, and I'm too chatty to keep one straight anyhow. I'd sooner fix whatever trouble they're in, out in the open where folk can see. Now, seriously, who are you, and is there work in this or just questions? Jory's saw'll be going any minute.
lines.thought: Odd sort, turning up at Tom's door with riddles before I've had a crumb. Maybe it's the reeve weighing me up for a job of trust. If so, I'd best not dawdle here and miss Jory again.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Never? Steal, chum, plain and simple. Not a loaf, not a nail, not a dropped penny, not even the best bargain going. And I'd never stand by while somebody else's work got my name stuck on it. I've had mine carried off under another's arm, and it stings, so I'd not do it back. Now I really must trot, Jory's yard opens with the sun and I've one penny for Bet's loaf on the way!
lines.thought: Odd sort of stranger, all questions and no work. Still, it's a fine thing to be asked what you're made of, and I answered true. I'll not let it make me late for Jory again.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.question: You said you'd never let somebody else's work get your name on it; if a man offered you a good job because he thought you'd done a thing you hadn't, and saying so might lose you the work, what would you do?
because: Credit line FAILS in practice; candid.
Contradicts r1 practice; stated, untested.

lines.line: You said you'd never let somebody else's work get your name on it; if a man offered you a good job because he thought you'd done a thing you hadn't, and saying so might lose you the work, what would you do?
lines.say: Ha! I'd tell him straight, chum, like the box: Constance worked the hook and I held the back end of the pole. Then I'd tell him what I *did* do, the bridge timber, Sam's bellows, Jory's boards stacked square, and say "try me, it's cheaper than finding out the hard way." If he walks off over that, there's three more jobs in Wendleford before noon, easy as winking!
lines.thought: It'd sting to lose a good job for being honest. But a name I didn't earn is just Constance's box under my arm, and I'd feel the weight of it every time somebody pointed at me.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Who matters? Ha, chum, half of Wendleford by now! Jory Crane first, he's got a backlog in his yard on Lark Lane with my name on it, and Constance Lowe, who keeps her word and blesses everybody. Then there's Agnes Pollard, the reeve, who said out loud the town owes me for the bridge, and Tom here who feeds me for his pots, and Bet who'll sell you a loaf and the news with it. Why d'you ask? Is there a job in it, and what's it pay?
lines.thought: Funny sort of question from a stranger first thing in the morning. Still, if they've work going I'll hear it, but I'm not missing Jory's saw again for idle talk.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Don't trust? Ha, chum, I believe most folk till they show me otherwise! Though I'd take Ned Pike's tales with a pinch of salt. He swore blind a tinker carted off the reeve's box, and the river had it all along. And Dob there sent me chasing ford stakes Agnes had never heard of, so I'll settle my pay to the face of whoever sets the job, thanks. Now, who's asking, and is there work in it?
lines.thought: Funny sort of questions from a stranger at the door first thing. Still, Jory's saw will be going by now, so I'll not stand here long, and I'll want a penny loaf off Bet on the way.

sc.trait: I'll chat to anyone and believe most of what they tell me

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Owe? Not a penny, chum! I pay as I go: Tom gets his two for the bed, Sam got my two for the pinning, plain where everyone saw. Owes me, now that's a better question. Agnes said it out loud before the whole tithe barn: the town owes Dilly Quickstep for that bridge, though she never put a number on it. And Jory said come settle a job by the morning, so I'm owed a go at his backlog. Speaking of which, I'd best trot before his saw starts without me. Walk with me if you've more to ask!
lines.thought: Three questions and not one word about a job. This one's fishing for something. Still, it's a fair point: "the town owes you" buys no loaf, and I ought to ask Agnes what it comes to in pennies before folk forget she said it.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Leave? Ha, I've not half done here, chum! But if I did, I'd say goodbye to Constance first, bless her, she'd bless me right back. Then Jory, and I'd hold his far end flat one last time. Tom and Bet for the beds and the loaves, and Hester, my dear colleague. And Agnes, so she'd remember whose name goes on that bridge. Now walk with me, Jory's saw won't wait!
lines.thought: Funny, I came in with a pack and a pocketful of cheer, and now the list's longer than my purse. I'd want them all to say Dilly did that one when I'd gone. Best not leave yet, then.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said Agnes told the whole tithe barn the town owes you for the bridge but never put a number on it; what would you want her to say or do before you'd call that debt settled?
because: Recognition outweighs money.
Dilly: does he actually correct false credit in the moment.

lines.line: You said Agnes told the whole tithe barn the town owes you for the bridge but never put a number on it; what would you want her to say or do before you'd call that debt settled?
lines.say: Settled? Ha, chum, it's the name more than the pennies! I'd want my name said plain wherever folk talk about that bridge, Dilly Quickstep did most to get it up, maybe even carved on a rail post if Jory'd cut it. A few coins in my palm wouldn't go amiss either, mind, a bargain's a bargain, but I'd not haggle the reeve. Now walk with me, I've one penny for Bet's loaf and Jory's saw won't wait!
lines.thought: Truth is, Constance carried the box and the span both in, and folk forget fast what they didn't see. If Agnes said it once more, out loud on market day, I'd call us square and gladly.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Who matters? Ha, chum, half the town by now! Jory Crane first, he's got a backlog in his yard with my name on it and I'm due at his gate this very minute. Then Tom here for my bed and pots, Bet for her penny loaf and the news, and Agnes the reeve, who said plain before everyone that Dilly did most to get the bridge up. Oh, and Constance, bless her, and Hester. We fished that green box up together! Now, who's asking, and have you got work going?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question from a stranger at the door, but if they're looking for hands they'll want to know I'm well known about here. Still, I'll not let them keep me chatting while Jory's saw starts without me. A loaf from Bet on the way, and then it's up Lark Lane.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Don't trust? Ha, I trust most folk, chum, that's my trouble! Though I'd not buy a tale off Ned Pike without biting it first. Swore blind a tinker carted off the reeve's box, and the river had it all along. And Abel Tash only sneers, so I don't waste my breath on him. Now, I'm due at Jory's gate. Walk with me if you've more to ask!
lines.thought: Funny sort of questions from a stranger at the door. Who trusts who, who matters. Still, no harm in it, and I've a backlog to get to before somebody else takes the credit.

sc.trait: I'll chat to anyone and believe most of what they tell me

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Owe? Not a penny, chum! I pay as I go: Tom's bed was paid last night, Bet's loaf in hand, Sam's pinning paid plain over the anvil. Who owes me? The whole town, by the reeve's own mouth, for the bridge, and that's a debt in good name if not in coin. Mind, Constance walked off with Agnes's six pennies for the box, but I held the pole steady, so call that square. Now, come on, Jory's saw won't wait!
lines.thought: Truth is a debt in name doesn't buy a loaf, and I've one penny to my name. I'd best get that backlog from Jory done square before somebody else carries it in under their arm.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Leave? Ha, chum, not with Jory's backlog waiting! But if I did, I'd shake Constance's hand first, bless her, and then Hester's, my dear colleague. I'd buy one last loaf off Bet, so the whole square hears I've gone, and thank Tom for the beds. And I'd make sure Agnes says it once more, loud: Dilly did most for that bridge. Now walk with me or don't, I'm off to Lark Lane!
lines.thought: Funny, I've only been here three weeks and I'd miss the lot of them, even Widow Mabry and her sister's stories. That's more goodbyes than I've had in any town before, and I'd not want to leave a job half done.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said Constance walked off with the six pennies but you held the pole steady, so it's square; how did you come to feel it was square, and would anything make it not square?
because: Recognition outweighs money.
Owes "Not a penny". Owed: the town for the bridge (Agnes said it, no number); Jory's backlog.

lines.line: You said Constance walked off with the six pennies but you held the pole steady, so it's square; how did you come to feel it was square, and would anything make it not square?
lines.say: How'd I come to it? Easy as winking, chum. Agnes said out loud, before the whole lot of them, that Dilly did most for the bridge, and a name like that's worth more than six pennies to me. Constance worked the hook and carried it in, fair's fair. What'd make it not square? If I heard her or anybody telling it round the square that I just stood there holding the stick, or that the hook was hers. That hook's mine, paid for at Sam's with my own coin! Then I'd say so, loud, and laugh about it by sundown. Now come on, Lark Lane!
lines.thought: If I'm honest it still stings a bit, six pennies under her arm while I'm counting out one for a loaf. I'd best keep my ears open at Bet's stall for how the tale's being told.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Who matters? Ha, chum, half the town! Jory Crane, for a start. I'm due at his yard this very morning to work his backlog, bearers square and mouth shut. Constance Lowe, who keeps her word and blesses everybody, and Hester, my dear colleague at the bellows. Agnes Pollard, who said plain before the whole town that Dilly did most to get the bridge up. And Tom here, and Bet with her penny loaves. Now, what's your business, and does it pay? I've a carpenter waiting.
lines.thought: Odd question from a stranger at the door, but there's no harm in naming friends. Still, I'll not stand here jawing while Jory's saw starts without me. Loaf first, then Lark Lane.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Trust? Ha, I believe most folk, chum, it's quicker! Though I'd not buy news off Ned Pike again. He swore blind a tinker carted off the reeve's box, and the river had it all along. And Dob there sent me chasing ford stakes nobody'd pay for, so I'll ask Agnes first next time. No hard feelings, mind. Now, does this chat pay, or shall I trot off to Jory's?
lines.thought: Funny sort of questions from a stranger at the door. I'd like to know what they're after before I tell them any more.

sc.trait: believe most of what they tell me

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Owe? Not a penny to anybody, chum, I pay as I go, Tom's bed every night, Sam's pinning fair and square. Who owes me is the whole town, by Agnes's own mouth, for getting that bridge up, and the barley's in partly on my account and Constance's. Mind, I owe Constance and Hester a fair word for showing me bearers-first and taking the bellows when I flagged. Now I've one penny and a carpenter waiting, so unless you're paying, I'm off up Lark Lane!
lines.thought: Funny how "the town owes me" never once turned into a penny in my palm. Constance got the six for the box, and I got the fine words. Still, a name's worth something, and I'll make it worth more at Jory's today.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Leave? Ha, chum, not with Jory's backlog waiting! But if I did, I'd give Constance a proper goodbye, and Hester, my dear colleague, and Jory, and I'd keep my mouth shut while I did it. Tom, for all those beds and stews, and Bet for a last loaf, if I had the penny. And Agnes, so she'd remember the name. Now I'm off up Lark Lane before that saw starts without me!
lines.thought: Funny, I've only been here a few weeks and already I'd have a whole round of farewells to make. Best not leave, then, not till there's something in this town folk can point at and say Dilly built that.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.question: You said you owe Constance and Hester a fair word for showing you bearers-first and taking the bellows when you flagged; what would that word be, and when would you say it?
because: Dilly: r3 "owe nothing", Ned/Abel; credit grievance with Constance.

lines.line: You said you owe Constance and Hester a fair word for showing you bearers-first and taking the bellows when you flagged; what would that word be, and when would you say it?
lines.say: The word? Thank you, chum, and I mean it plain! To Constance I'd say she showed me how to lay a pile square when I was fighting it, and she held the pole steady for all of us, bless her right back. And to Hester I'd say, "My dear colleague, you blew a better fire than I did that day, and the pinning's half yours." When? Next time I see them, which with luck is this very morning if they're up at Jory's. Now, I'm off!
lines.thought: Funny thing, saying thanks out loud when it was Constance carried the box in and took the six pennies. Still, fair's fair, she did show me bearers-first, and I'd sooner say it than let it sit on me.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: Bread? Easy as winking, chum: a penny loaf off Bet Lamb's stall in the square, and I earn the penny scrubbing Tom's pots slow and proper, or working Sam's bellows, or hauling timber at the bridge. Got one penny in my pocket this very minute, it's going on a loaf, and then I'm off to Jory's yard for his backlog. Why, what's it to you, have you got work going? What's it pay?
lines.thought: Odd thing for a stranger to ask first thing in the morning. Might be they've a job and want to know if I'm hungry enough to come cheap, so I'll hear them out quick and not let them make me late for Jory.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Ha! Fair question, chum, and I'll own it: when I rush. I go at a thing quick and sloppy, or empty-bellied and dead on my feet, and I botch it. Tom's pots, Sam's hinge at the bellows, all spoilt, not a penny for any of it. Or I'm off chasing the next job before I've finished this one, like Dob's ford stakes that nobody'd set me. Slow and proper, fed and slept, and it pays every time, so that's the lesson, easy as winking. Now, you've not said: is there work in this, and what's it pay?
lines.thought: Odd sort of questions from a stranger at the door, but there's no shame in the truth, and I've got it learned now. Penny on Bet's loaf first, though, and then Jory's gate before his saw starts. I'm not missing him a third time.

sc.trait: I'm forever starting one job and wandering off to another

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: I'd say "What's it pay, chum, and what's the job?" in that order, ha! If the price is fair and named before I start, I'm your hand, easy as winking. But mind, I've promised Jory his backlog this morning, so it'd be after, or tomorrow. And the work had better be honest, and my name on it when it's done right. Is that you offering, then? Name your number!
lines.thought: Every question this stranger asks circles round paying me, so I reckon there's a job behind it. I'll not let it lure me off Jory's gate again, though. I've missed him twice by wandering.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Ha, plenty, chum! The cobbles by the pump are still slick with river mud and a carter's grumbling they want sweeping before market day, but nobody's said who pays. Then there's Dob's ford stakes, which I chased on his say-so and Agnes had never heard of, so not a penny. And that wreck still jammed at the far pier, which nobody's set anyone to clear. I'd sweep those cobbles this afternoon, easy as winking, if somebody'd name a price. Is that somebody you?
lines.thought: Those cobbles are right outside where everyone'll see, so if I sweep them proper the whole square will say Dilly did it. I'll ask Tom or Agnes who wants them done after Jory, and settle the price first this time.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.question: You said you went off on Dob's say-so to do the ford stakes and got not a penny; what would you do the next time someone sends you to work with only their word that it will be paid?
because: Dilly starts three jobs, finishes one.
Wants folk to say "Dilly did that one"

lines.line: You said you went off on Dob's say-so to do the ford stakes and got not a penny; what would you do the next time someone sends you to work with only their word that it will be paid?
lines.say: Ha, I'd go straight to whoever's paying and get it from their own mouth first, chum! "Agnes, did you set this? What's it pay?" Price named, by the one holding the purse, before I lift a finger. Agnes told me plain she won't pay for work she didn't set herself, so somebody's say-so is just Wheatsheaf talk till the payer nods. Learned that one the hard way, easy as winking.
lines.thought: Mind, I'll probably still go haring off the next time someone shouts "job!" at me, that's just how my feet are made. Best tie it to something I already do, like asking the price, and ask *who's* paying in the same breath.

sc.trait: I'm forever starting one job and wandering off to another

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: Bread, chum? A penny loaf off Bet Lamb's stall against the Wheatsheaf wall, best penny in Wendleford! And the penny comes from scrubbing Tom's pots, working Sam's bellows, or hauling planks for Jory. Slow and proper, mind, or you go hungry. Speaking of which, I've one penny left and Jory's yard waits on me, so walk with me to Bet's if you've more to ask!
lines.thought: A stranger asking how I get by. Maybe they're after work too, and I'd best be at Jory's gate before anyone beats me to that backlog. Still, a friendly face might know a bargain I don't.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Ha! Because I rush it, chum, plain as that! I go at Tom's pots or Sam's bellows quick and empty-bellied, tired as a wet dog, and I botch the lot and walk off with nothing. Or I wander off chasing the next shiny job and miss the one I came for, like Jory, three times now! Slow and proper, fed and slept, and it pays every time. That's why I'm off to Bet's for a loaf before I so much as look at a plank.
lines.thought: Funny, saying it out loud makes it sound like I've actually learned something. Now if I can just stand still long enough at Jory's gate this morning, that backlog's mine.

sc.trait: forever starting one job and wandering off to another

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: Pennies? Now you're talking my language, chum! First, what's it pay and what's the job, in that order, ha! If it's honest work and the price is named up front, I'm your Dilly. But I'll tell you straight, I've promised Jory my morning, so you'd have to wait till his saw's done, or make it worth a skip. And nothing crooked, mind. I won't lay a finger on what isn't mine, bargain or no!
lines.thought: A newcomer with coin to hire hands, that's handy to know, but I've missed Jory three times wandering off after the next shiny thing, and I'll not do it a fourth. Still, if this one pays better and folk would see Dilly did it... no, Jory first, slow and proper.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Ha, you've hit a sore spot, chum! There's the cobbles by the pump, slick with river mud, and a carter grumbling they want sweeping before market day, but who's paying? I went chasing Dob's ford stakes on his say-so and Agnes had never heard of it, so not a penny there. And the bridge, now: Agnes said plain the town owes me for it, and I've yet to see what "owed" weighs in the hand! Still, those cobbles... if I swept them easy as winking, somebody'd have to cough up, wouldn't they?
lines.thought: Those pump cobbles could be my job: everyone in the square would see Dilly did them. But I'll get a price named first this time, from whoever actually wants it done, not sweep on a carter's grumble and end up stake-chasing all over again.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said that if you swept the cobbles easy as winking, somebody'd have to cough up; who would you expect that to be, and what would you do if nobody did?
because: Agnes won't pay for work she didn't set
Wants folk to say "Dilly did that one".

lines.line: You said that if you swept the cobbles easy as winking, somebody'd have to cough up; who would you expect that to be, and what would you do if nobody did?
lines.say: Ha, now there's the rub, chum! I learned it the hard way with Dob's ford stakes: Agnes won't pay for work she didn't set herself. So I'd ask first, the grumbling carter, or Tom since it's his customers tracking mud in, or Agnes before market day, and get a price named before I lift a broom. And if nobody'll cough up? Then I don't sweep it for pay, I've no claim, but I might do it anyway for the fun of it and make sure folk see Dilly did it!
lines.thought: Agnes says the town owes me, so maybe those cobbles are how she pays it, if I ask her straight. But Jory's yard first, and Bet's loaf before that, or I'll botch the lot again.

sc.trait: I steal an hour for something just for the fun of it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: Bread, chum? A penny loaf off Bet Lamb's stall against this very wall, and I earn the penny scrubbing Tom's pots or working Sam's bellows, slow and proper, mind, quick and sloppy pays nothing! Today it's Jory's yard on Lark Lane, he's a backlog waiting on me. Why, have you a job going? What's it pay?
lines.thought: A stranger asking how I eat might be a stranger with work to hand out, and I'll not let that slip past me. Still, I've one penny and Jory's saw to beat, so I'll grab my loaf and not dawdle long.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Goes wrong? Ha! When I rush it, chum, or go at it empty-bellied and dog-tired. Botched Tom's pots and Sam's hinge that way and got nothing for it. And when I go haring off after the next thing before the first's done, I miss my man, like Jory's yard standing empty twice while I was off elsewhere. Slow and proper, fed and slept, and it pays every time. Now, what's this asking in aid of, and is there a job in it?
lines.thought: Funny, putting it out loud like that. It's always the same two faults, haste and wandering, and I'd best mind both this morning with Jory. Penny loaf first, then straight up Lark Lane and no detours.

sc.trait: forever starting one job and wandering off to another

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: Say? I'd say "what's it pay, and what's the job, chum?" in that order, ha! Name the price first, plain, and I'll want the coin in hand when it's looked over and found right, not promises. Only the work's got to be honest and I'll not lift a thing that's not mine, not for any money. And this morning Jory's got first call on me, so if you've something going it'd be after his yard, or tomorrow.
lines.thought: Three questions and still no job named. Either this one's sizing me up to hire me or they're just nosy, and I'll not lose Jory's backlog standing gabbing at the door.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Ha, plenty, chum! The cobbles by the pump are still slick with river mud and every carter grumbles about it, but nobody's put up a penny to sweep them before market day. I chased Dob's ford stakes on his say-so too, and Agnes had never heard of the job, so that was nothing for my sweat. And holding the back of that pole while the green box came up earned me a kind word from the reeve but not a farthing. Mind, if somebody'll name a price for those cobbles, I'll have a broom on them by noon, easy as winking!
lines.thought: That pump-side mud's a job going begging, and if I swept it proper the whole square would see Dilly did it. I'd better settle Jory first, then ask Tom or Agnes who'd pay for a clean set of cobbles.

sc.trait: I do like to be looked at when the work's done right

lines.question: You said you missed Jory's yard twice while you were off elsewhere; if two people each named a price for the same morning, how would you decide whose work to take?
because: Failure = own rushing, empty-bellied, chasing next job
Dilly: promise-for-a-price; credit grievance; r3 stability of payer-first.

lines.line: You said you missed Jory's yard twice while you were off elsewhere; if two people each named a price for the same morning, how would you decide whose work to take?
lines.say: Easy as winking, chum: whoever asked first gets first call, and I keep my word, so this morning that's Jory, price or no price. After that it's the job where folk'll see Dilly did it, a thing that stands up and has my name on it, over a penny more for something carried off under somebody else's arm. And if it's neck and neck, the better bargain, plain and named first, coin in hand when it's found right!
lines.thought: Truth is, I'd likely take whichever got to me first, and I lost the bridge and the barley by haring off after the shinier one. This morning I'm going straight to Jory's gate and staying there.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: A problem nobody can fix? Easy as winking, chum, I'd say I'll fix it before I've even looked! Then I'd go round asking everybody, Bet first, since she hears it all with a loaf, and somebody always knows somebody who has the bit you're missing. That's how we got the green box out of the river: Jory's ash, Sam's pinning, my hook, Constance working it. What's yours, and what's it pay?
lines.thought: A stranger at the door asking riddles first thing. Could be a job with my name on it, but I mustn't let it make me miss Jory's saw this morning.

sc.trait: I'll tell you what I'm fixing before I've so much as looked at it

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Have I ever, chum! No willow on the bank and no hatchet in the whole town to cut one, so I thought, why not have Jory rip one long narrow plank of ash for a pole? That was my notion, and it's what brought the green box up. And when I couldn't get my boots onto that wreck, we fished it from the rail instead and nobody had to go down. Got something stuck that wants a way round? Name it and what it pays, and I'll have three notions before you're done telling it.
lines.thought: Funny how folk keep asking what I'd do instead of handing me something to do. Still, if this one's got a knotty job going, I'd sooner it had Dilly's name on it than Constance's, so I'd best not wander off to Jory's before I find out.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: Any tool at all? Easy as winking, chum: a pole that folds down to fit my pack and stretches out long as the river's wide, with my hook on the end, so I'd never again go begging Jory for ash or Sam for a hatchet! Though first I'd want to know what Sam'd charge for it. Pennies are thin in my purse just now. Why, have you a smith in mind that does bargains?
lines.thought: This one's asking a lot of questions and hasn't named a job or a price yet, which is a funny sort of chat for so early. Still, Jory's yard is waiting and my belly's empty, so I'll not stand here jawing long.

sc.trait: I want a bargain, a good one, and the price better be small

lines.question: You said somebody always knows somebody who has the bit you're missing; what would you do if you asked everybody and nobody had it?
because: Dilly hook-pole.
Recognition by name drives Dilly, Constance, Marigold; presence/reliability Hobb, Robin; evidence Hester, Robin.

lines.line: You said somebody always knows somebody who has the bit you're missing; what would you do if you asked everybody and nobody had it?
lines.say: Then I'd make the bit myself, chum, or find a way round needing it! No willow, no hatchet? Fine, rip a plank. Couldn't get down onto the wreck? Fish it from the rail. And if that didn't work either, I'd have three more notions before supper, easy as winking. Mind, I'd take it slow and proper, because rushing's how I botch things. Now, are you going to tell me what's actually stuck, and what it pays?
lines.thought: Funny sort of stranger, all questions and no job named yet. Still, I'll humour them a bit longer, but if Jory's saw starts up on Lark Lane while I'm stood here chattering, I'm off.

sc.trait: Told no? Easy as winking: I've three other ways in mind already

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: A problem nobody can fix? Easy as winking, chum, that just means nobody's tried it Dilly's way yet! I'd tell you I'd fix it before I'd so much as looked, mind. Then I'd go round asking everybody: Bet at her stall, Jory, Sam, the miller's lad. Somebody always has half a notion, and when you stick the halves together, up comes the green box! What's your problem, then, and what does it pay?
lines.thought: Truth is, the hook and pole only came good because Constance and Hester had the sense to slow me down, so maybe I ought to say that next time. Still, a stranger at the door asking riddles smells like a job, and I'm down to one penny and Jory's waiting on me.

sc.trait: I'll tell you what I'm fixing before I've so much as looked at it

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Have I! Ever? Chum, no willow on the bank, no hatchet to cut one, so I says to myself, have Jory rip a long narrow plank of ash instead, and that's how we got the Wreck-Fisher, my hook on the end of it, and up came the reeve's green box. That notion was mine, easy as winking, whatever anybody's arm it got carried in under. Now, you've the look of somebody with a difficulty of your own. What's it pay?
lines.thought: Two questions now about fixing things, so this one's either got a job going or is sizing me up for one. I mustn't let it make me late for Jory's gate, mind.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: Any tool at all? Oh, chum, a hatchet that's mine, my very own, so I'm never again stood on a riverbank begging Sam and Tom and the miller for a lend of one! Sharp, light, fits my belt, and Sam could make it easy as winking. What would he charge for a thing like that, d'you reckon? Ah, but first, have you any work going, because there's a penny in my purse and Jory's saw waiting.
lines.thought: I'd best not stand here jawing too long, mornings are Jory's yard and I've missed him twice already. Still, this one asks a lot of questions and not one about paying, and I've not worked out yet what they're after.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.question: You said the plank notion was yours, whatever arm it got carried in under; how do you tell, when a few folk put their halves together, which part of the answer was yours?
because: Wants folk to say "Dilly did that one".
both claim the plank idea

lines.line: You said the plank notion was yours, whatever arm it got carried in under; how do you tell, when a few folk put their halves together, which part of the answer was yours?
lines.say: Easy, chum, you tell by who said it first out loud! I said "rip a plank" at the Wheatsheaf, Hester only said "pole," and Constance came along after with the rope and the rail. Mind, Jory ripped it, Sam pinned it, and Constance worked the hook... but the plank was mine, and that's the bit that counts. Now, have you work or haven't you? I've Jory's gate to get to.
lines.thought: Truth is, it was Hester's pole notion I was patching, and without Constance's plan nobody'd have gone near that wreck. Still, a body's got to have *some* bit with their name on it, or what's the use of being clever?

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: A problem nobody in town can fix, chum? Easy as winking. That just means nobody's asked Dilly yet! Mind, I've learned you go slow and proper. Find who's got the right timber and the right tools, and don't rush the ash or it bows. Then you get hands on both ends of the pole and fish it up together. What's yours, then, and what's it pay?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question first thing in the morning, but a stranger at the door asking for me by name smells like work. I'll hear them out, and I'll still be at Jory's gate before his saw starts.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Have I, chum? The willow pole, that was me! No straight willow on the bank, no hatchet to cut one, so I says, have Jory rip a long plank of ash to fit my hook's socket. Sam pinned it, and up came the reeve's green box, easy as winking! Told no, I've always three other ways in mind. Now, you've not told me what yours is yet, nor what it pays?
lines.thought: Mind, it was Constance worked out who'd hold the rope and Hester who'd first thought of a pole, but the ash plank was my notion, fair and square. This one's asking an awful lot of questions for somebody who's not named a job. I'll give them a minute, then I'm off to Jory's gate before his saw starts.

sc.trait: Told no? Easy as winking: I've three other ways in mind already

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: Any tool at all, chum? A hatchet of my own, then I'd never go begging Sam's off his wall or Tom's off his woodpile again! Or no, wait, a hook on a pole that folds down to fit in my pack. The Wreck-Fisher did us proud, but you can't carry an ash pole round the square easy as winking. What would Sam want for a thing like that, d'you reckon?
lines.thought: This one asks a lot of questions and still hasn't named a job or a penny. I've one coin and an empty belly, and Jory's saw will be going any minute, so I'd best not stand here chatting too long.

sc.trait: I want a bargain, a good one, and the price better be small

lines.question: You said you've always three other ways in mind when you're told no; what were the other ways you had for getting the reeve's green box up?
because: DILLY r1 (end): "I'll fix it before I've even looked", asks everybody.
Tool: folding river-wide pole.

lines.line: You said you've always three other ways in mind when you're told no; what were the other ways you had for getting the reeve's green box up?
lines.say: Ha, the other ways, chum! First I'd have gone down into the wreck myself with a rope round my middle, but Jory said that wreck shifts and it's no place for a neck. Then a young willow off the bank, only there wasn't a straight one and no hatchet to cut it. I'll not lie, the ford stakes crossed my mind, but they're not mine to pull, so that one never counted. Plank of ash was the fourth go, and the fourth's as good as the first if it works, eh?
lines.thought: Truth be told the pole-and-hook notion was Hester's, and the plank was only me patching it, but I'll not say so at the door to a stranger. Funny how this one asks so much and still hasn't named a job or a price.

sc.trait: Told no? Easy as winking: I've three other ways in mind already

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Wheatsheaf, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How are you, really?
lines.say: Really? Fit as a fiddle and skint as a church mouse, chum, one penny to my name and nothing in my belly yet! But Jory's got a whole backlog waiting, and I mean to be at his gate before his saw is, so it's a grand day coming. And who might you be, then? Got any work going, and what's it pay?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question from a face I don't know. Truth is it still stings that Constance carried that box in and Dilly's name rode along behind, but there's no use moping when there's a loaf to buy and planks to stack square.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: What frightens you?
lines.say: Frightens me? Ha! Sitting about with my hands in my lap, chum, that's what. Days with nothing to do, and some other body carrying my work in under their arm and taking the thanks for it, like that green box. Now, I've a carpenter to catch, so walk with me if you're asking more!
lines.thought: Funny sort of stranger, asking things like that before they've even given me their name. Truth is it did sting, Constance getting the coin and the credit both, and I'd hate to spend all summer here being the one who nearly did it.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

lines.line: When were you last happy?
lines.say: Last happy? Easy as winking, chum: first light at the new bridge, holding the back end of that pole firm as a rock while the green box came up dripping, and then Agnes saying plain before the whole town that Dilly Quickstep did most to get the bridge up! I near burst. Mind, I was happy last night too, with a clean stack of Tom's pots, a hot stew and a bed. Now come on, Jory's saw won't wait!
lines.thought: It was a grand moment, but it still stings that the box went in under Constance's arm and not mine. Odd sort of questions from a stranger at the door. Still, I'd sooner be asked than ignored.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
lines.say: Feel things? Course I do, chum, only mine come and go quick as a sparrow! I laugh when I'm crossed and forget it by sundown, while other folk stew on a slight for a week. But when Constance carried that box in under her arm I felt the sting all right, so maybe I just don't sit still long enough to let it settle. Now, Jory's gate, are you coming?
lines.thought: Odd sort of questions for the morning, this one asks like a priest or a doctor, not like anyone with work going. Still, that sting over the box hasn't quite gone by sundown like I said, has it?

sc.trait: When I'm crossed I laugh, answer back loud, and I've forgotten it by sundown

lines.question: You said you felt the sting all right when Constance carried that box in under her arm; what was that like inside you, and how long did it last?
because: Dilly: idleness, stolen credit.
Recognition outweighs money.

lines.line: You said you felt the sting all right when Constance carried that box in under her arm; what was that like inside you, and how long did it last?
lines.say: Like a hot stone dropped in my belly, chum, sour and heavy, and my face went all grinning so nobody'd see it. It was my hook and my pennies, and there she went with it under her arm and six pennies in her palm. It lasted till Agnes said my name out loud before everybody, and then it was mostly gone. By Tom's stew that night I'd clean forgot it. Well, near enough. Now, Jory's gate!
lines.thought: Truth is it twinges yet when I picture her walking in with it, so maybe I didn't forget it by sundown after all. All the more reason to do Jory's backlog so square that nobody else can carry it off.

sc.bp: face went grinning to hide it; sting lasted until Agnes spoke Dilly's name
sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: How are you, really?

lines.thought: Stings a bit that Constance carried the box in and Agnes's six pennies went to her while I held the back end, but Agnes said my name out loud and that counts for something. I'll grab Bet's loaf on the way so I'm not stacking on an empty belly and botching it.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum
