lines.say: Frightens me? Ha! Sitting about with my hands in my lap, chum, that's the worst of it, and some other beggar carrying in the thing I fixed under their arm and taking the six pennies for it. Now, I've a penny for Bet's loaf and Jory's saw'll be going any minute, so walk with me if you've more to ask!
lines.thought: That box stings worse than I let on. Dilly held the pole, but it's Constance they'll remember. And this one asks odd questions for a stranger who's not offered work. Still, a friendly face is a friendly face.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

lines.line: When were you last happy?
lines.say: Happy? Ha! First light at the new bridge, chum, holding the back end of that pole firm as a rock when the green box came up, and then Agnes saying plain before everybody that Dilly Quickstep did most to get the bridge up. Mind, Tom's stew last night after a clean stack of pots weren't half bad either. Now come on, Bet's loaf won't buy itself!
lines.thought: Funny how the happiest bit wasn't the box at all but Agnes saying my name out loud. Still, I'd have liked those six pennies in my own palm, and I mean to make Jory's backlog something folk can point at and say I did.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
lines.say: The way other folk do? Couldn't say, chum. I've only ever been inside my own head! Mine come quick and go quick: I'll laugh off a telling-off and forget it by sundown, while Constance blesses every soul and broods on it like a hen on eggs. But that sting when she carried the box in under her arm? I felt that one proper, I'll tell you. Now step lively, Jory's saw won't wait!
lines.thought: Funny sort of question to ask a body at a tavern door, but it's stuck in me like a splinter. Maybe I rush about so I don't have to sit long enough to find out.

sc.bp: Constance broods on telling-offs like a hen on eggs
sc.trait: I've forgotten it by sundown

lines.question: You said sitting about with your hands in your lap is the worst of it; when you have to sit like that, what does it feel like inside you, and what do you do with it?
because: Dilly: does he ever fail; sitting still.
Fear: idle hands; someone else taking thanks "like that green box".

lines.line: You said sitting about with your hands in your lap is the worst of it; when you have to sit like that, what does it feel like inside you, and what do you do with it?
lines.say: Inside? Like a kettle with the lid held down, chum, all fizz and rattle and nowhere to go. My feet start tapping, my fingers want a rope or a pot, and I start thinking the whole town's getting on without me. So I grab whatever's nearest. I shelled Widow Mabry's beans yesterday waiting on Jory, and I'd have counted cobbles if she'd had none!
lines.thought: Funny thing is, the times I sat on my hands and went slow were the times I got paid, and every botch I've made came from the fizz. Maybe the kettle wants learning to simmer.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

lines.line: You said anger flares up and is gone by sundown, yet the green box going up the square still stung a bit; how long does a sting like that stay with you, and what do you do with it?
lines.say: Ha, caught me fair, chum! The temper's gone by sundown, sure as cockcrow, but a sting like that lingers a few days, sort of a splinter, and the cure's to get my hands into the next job and do it square enough that nobody can carry it off under their arm. So that's where I'm off now, to Jory's backlog, bearers first. Walk with me if you like, but I'll not stand here chewing on it while his saw's going without me!
lines.thought: Odd sort, asking after my insides instead of my price. Truth is, I'll not hold it against Constance, she earned her six pennies, but I mean to be standing right beside whatever comes next when folk start pointing.

lines.line: What brings you here?
lines.say: Work, chum, that's what! Came in a few days back with a pack and a grin, and since then I've hauled bridge timber, pinned my own hook on the pole that fished up the reeve's green box, and scrubbed half of Tom's pots. Now I'm off to Jory's yard, he's got a backlog with my name on it. What about you, got anything wants doing, and what's it pay?
lines.thought: A stranger asking after me first thing. Could be a job, could be nothing, but I'll not stand chatting so long that Jory's saw starts without me. One penny left, and that's Bet's loaf on the way.

lines.line: "I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?

lines.line: Is there anything in how they were made that doesn't fit?

Dilly's note says coins burn a hole in their pocket and tomorrow can look after itself, but the world's pennies are so tight that they've had to count every one, and the thrift I've played doesn't match that. They're also meant to steal an hour for fun most days, and that has almost never happened because pots, bed and bread eat every day. The biggest misfit is that they want to be *the* one who fixed it, alone, in a town where nearly every real job, the bridge, the barley, the box, gets done by several hands together. That last one I'd keep, though. It's the friction that gives Dilly a story.

lines.say: Tomorrow, chum? Easy as winking: I wake up with that green box already handed to the reeve and six pennies jingling alongside my four, and the whole square saying "that's Dilly Quickstep, that is." Then a sheaf or two of Dunn's barley under my arm before the rain, a hot loaf at a bargain price, and not one minute spent sitting on my hands. Oh, and a good laugh somewhere in it, I always find one!
lines.thought: That's tomorrow's, but I've not so much as sniffed for that box today, and my belly's growling. Best ask Bet what a loaf costs and what she's heard about the bridge that night, both in one go.

lines.line: You said you trust nearly everybody until they give you cause not to; what would count as cause for you?

Or somebody nicking what isn't theirs, and I'll not stand for that, not even for a bargain. Short-weighting me on a loaf'd count too, though I'd laugh it off by sundown and buy from them again if the price was right.
lines.thought: Funny how many questions this one's asking, and none of them about pots or pennies. I'd best keep my eyes on that wage box, in case they're after the six pennies themselves.

lines.line: Who here would you trust, and why?
lines.say: Trust? Oh, near enough everybody, chum, I'm an easy one that way! Tom Harrow gave me a bed for my pennies fair and square, and Bet's loaves are honest weight, I'd wager. She hears all the talk in the square too, so if anyone knows where that green box went it's her. Agnes Pollard put her reward up in plain ink for all to read, and that's good enough for me. Now Ned there, I'd trust him to sell me a bargain, I just might give it a good shake first!
lines.thought: Truth is I'll believe most anyone till they cross me, and that's served me fine so far. Still, a box of wages doesn't just float off on its own. Somebody here knows more than they're saying, and Bet's the one to sweet-talk it out of over a loaf.

lines.say: Easy as winking, chum: the broken bridge, south of here! Agnes had the box with her right there the night the flood came, so either it went into the Wend or it's snagged somewhere downstream in the reeds, maybe caught up by the ford stakes. A loaf-sized box bound in iron doesn't float far, does it? So I'll walk the bank from the bridge down to the ford and have a good poke about, though I'll ask Bet over a loaf first whether anyone's been seen grubbing about down there.
lines.thought: If somebody's already fished it out and kept quiet, that's a different kettle of fish, and I'd want to know who before I go shouting about it. Either way, I'm not having some other clever clogs walk off with that reward while I'm stood here jawing.

lines.thought: Truth is, it stung more than I let on, and it wasn't the only time either. Maybe I ought to ask the reeve straight out how she pays before I break my back for her.

lines.line: You said you were in the square the night the bridge went and there's an itch about it, like you saw something worth noticing; what do you remember of that night, and what do you make of the itch?
lines.say: That night? Rain like a bucket tipped over, chum, folk shouting, and a roar off the river like a herd of cattle coming down the lane. Then a great crack, and the bridge was gone. Past that it's all a blur of running and wet boots, and I'll not dress it up and tell you I saw the reeve's green box floating by, because I didn't, not that I can swear to. The itch? Could be nothing but nerves, could be something. If you've a mind to help me scratch it, we'll split whatever it turns up. Fair's fair!
lines.thought: Six pennies is a fine reward, and "the one who found the reeve's box" has a lovely ring to it. I'll ask Bet over a loaf what folk saw that night, and maybe walk down to the broken bridge and see if the place jogs anything loose.

lines.line: You said that if somebody tells you that you promised them something, you'll take their word and get it done; what would you do if their word and your own memory pulled different ways?
lines.say: Ha! Then I'd laugh first and squint at 'em second, chum. If it's a job of work they say I promised, I'll likely just do it, since I'd rather be busy than right, and my memory's a leaky bucket anyhow. But if it's pennies they say I owe, or they're telling me *they* fixed what I fixed, then we'll go ask Tom or Bet together and settle it square, loud as you like.
lines.thought: Funny thing is, I'd trust a stranger's word over my own head half the time, and that's maybe not so clever. Still, nobody's walking off with my credit, whatever I've forgotten.

sc.trait: I can't stand somebody else walking off with my credit

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
lines.say: Yesterday? Ha, chum, it's a blur, the way most days are with me! Up early, I'll tell you that much, poked about the square, asked Bet what a loaf goes for, and read the reeve's notice about that green box till I near had it by heart. Then I slept like a stone at the Wheatsheaf, bed's paid for, two more nights. Now, you wouldn't be wanting a job done, would you? Easy as winking, whatever it is.
lines.thought: Odd sort of question from a stranger, wanting my whole day laid out like washing, and truth is I can't rightly recall the half of it. Still, a body who asks questions might have work, or know where that wage box went.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: Ha! Chum, if I could remember what I've forgotten I'd not have forgotten it, would I? But now you mention it, the night the bridge went, I was right there in the square with all the shouting and the water, and it's all a jumble, lanterns and folk running. Funny thing to ask a stranger, mind. Why, what've you heard?
lines.thought: That night does sit in me like a pebble in a boot, and the reeve had that green box right there by the bridge. If there's something rattling about in my head that'd lead me to six pennies and my name on everyone's lips, I'd best go stand by the broken bridge and see if it shakes loose.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
lines.say: Jump? Ha, chum, all the time! I start mending a gate at breakfast, wander off after a dog, and next I look up the sun's gone round and I've no notion where the morning went. That's just being busy, that is. Speaking of which, you're asking a lot of questions for someone who hasn't said what they pay. Got any work, or shall I go try the bridge?
lines.thought: Odd sort, this one, asking about gaps and jumps like they're fishing for something. Still, the barley won't cut itself and Bet's loaves are getting cold, so I'll not stand here puzzling all morning.

sc.trait: I'm forever starting one job and wandering off to another

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
lines.say: Sure? Sure as a fair price, chum, which is to say mostly! If I'm not certain I ask somebody. Tom Harrow'll tell you I paid him for two nights, Bet'll tell you I asked after her loaves, and the notice board's right there if I've got the reeve's words wrong. Folk remember for you if you let them. Now, all this talk's making me hungry. Bet, what's a loaf this morning?
lines.thought: Odd sort of questions, these, like they're poking for a crack. But my pocket says four pennies and my belly says no breakfast, and I trust those two more than any stranger.

sc.trait: I'll chat to anyone and believe most of what they tell me

lines.question: You said "Folk remember for you if you let them." Has anyone ever remembered something about you that you'd not have said yourself, and what did you do about it?
because: Others' word wins when cheap; witnesses when money or credit is at stake.
r2: promises box by sundown. r3: asks what the reeve pays; a Hollin Cross man left owing three pennies, laughed off ("one sour plum").

lines.line: You said "Folk remember for you if you let them." Has anyone ever remembered something about you that you'd not have said yourself, and what did you do about it?
lines.say: Ha! Once or twice, chum. A fellow in the last town swore I'd promised to mend his cart wheel and then walked off to help with a barn raising, and blow me if he wasn't right. I laughed, went back and did the wheel, and charged him half for his trouble remembering it. Now, Bet, that loaf?
lines.thought: Truth is, I've likely left a trail of half-mended things behind me in every town I've passed through. Best not to have this one asking after the night of the flood too closely, not until I know what I did with myself in all that jumble.

sc.bp: a cart-wheel promise in the last town; a barn raising; going back to fix the wheel and charging half
sc.trait: I promise things grandly and lose track of them just as quick

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: A person? Ha! Chum, I've got four pennies, an empty belly and a wage box to find. That's about as person as it gets! Wondering's for folk who sit about. Speaking of which, you don't happen to know what Bet's asking for a loaf this morning, do you?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to put to a stranger first thing. Maybe they're one of Mother Wick's lot, or just short of sleep. Either way, I'd sooner be fixing something than chewing on that.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: A made thing? Well, somebody made the bridge, chum, and the flood unmade it quick enough! Made or not, the cobbles are wet, Bet's bread smells warm, and Farmer Dunn's barley won't cut itself before the rain. You can puzzle over it all you like, but I'm off to find work, so if you've a spare pair of hands, come along!
lines.thought: Odd sort, sitting about asking riddles while there's a wage box missing. Mind, if anyone knew the town's secret workings, they might know where a green iron box washed up.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Prove it? Ha! Chum, if I stub my toe on a made cobble it smarts just the same, and if I find that green box Agnes'll pay me six real pennies for it. Proof enough for me! Now, if you want to *help* prove something, we could wade the ford and get Dunn's barley in before the rain. That'd prove we're useful, at least.
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to sit on, and they keep circling it like a dog at a gatepost. Still, a body who asks that much might know a thing or two about where a box could wash up after a flood. I'll keep them talking.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Tomorrow? Ha! Tomorrow I'll be up before the cock's done crowing, same as ever, chum. Made town or real one, those pots at the Wheatsheaf still want washing and that barley still wants cutting before the rain. Wouldn't change a thing, except maybe I'd ask whoever made it what they charge for a bridge!
lines.thought: Odd sort, sitting about asking riddles while there's work going begging. Still, it's a fair question, and the honest answer's no. I'd still want my name on whatever gets fixed.

sc.trait: I'm up and doing before the cock's done crowing

lines.question: You said Agnes would pay you six real pennies for the green box, so what makes a penny real to you?
because: DILLY QUICKSTEP: Odd-job man, breezy, boastful. Four pennies. Aims: green wage box (reeve's six-penny reward), barley, bridge, loaf.
Evidence accepted: none offered; anchors are body, coin, debts, work.

lines.line: You said Agnes would pay you six real pennies for the green box, so what makes a penny real to you?
lines.say: Real? Ha! A penny's real when Bet'll swap me a loaf for it, chum, that's the whole trick of it! If she takes it and I eat, it's real as rain. Speaking of which, I've four of 'em jingling and nothing in my belly, so I'm off to test one on her right now. Coming?
lines.thought: Odd sort, this one, all questions and no hands. Still, they got me thinking a penny's only worth what somebody'll give you for it, which is a fine thing to keep in mind when I'm haggling with Bet.

sc.trait: Coins burn a hole in my pocket

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: A person? Ha! Chum, I've got four pennies, an empty belly and a bridge's worth of trouble to sort out. That's about as person as it gets! Now, you haven't seen an iron-bound box, green, size of a loaf, have you? Six pennies reward, and I'll split it fair if you point me right.
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to drop on a body before breakfast. Maybe they sit with Mother Wick by the shrine. Never mind; I'd sooner ask Bet what a loaf costs than stand about wondering what I am.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: Made thing? Chum, every town's a made thing! Somebody made that pump, somebody made Bet's loaves, and somebody's going to make that bridge again, and it'll be me, easy as winking. If it only *looks* like a town, it smells an awful lot like warm bread for a pretend, so what's a loaf cost in a made-up place, eh? Same four pennies, I'll wager.
lines.thought: Odd one, this, all riddles and no work, but they've got a still way of sitting that makes me wonder what they've seen. Still, riddles don't fill a belly or find a green box, so I'll be off to Bet's before the morning's gone.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Prove it? Chum, I'd bite Bet's loaf, and if it fills my belly it's real enough for me! Or I'd wade that ford stake to stake, and if the cold bites my shins, there's your proof, easy as winking. Now look, you've got a thinking sort of face, so help me think where a green box goes when a river takes it, eh?
lines.thought: Odd duck, this one, chewing on questions you can't eat or spend. Still, a box the size of a loaf would sink or snag, wouldn't it? Somewhere downstream, by the ford maybe, and that's worth a look before noon.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Change it? Not a hair, chum! Real or made, tomorrow there's barley to cut before the rain, a box to find, and pots in Tom's scullery if the rest goes sour. Matter of fact, I'd likely do it all twice as fast, just in case somebody's watching. Now, I'm off to Bet for a loaf and a bit of gossip. Coming?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to sit and chew on, and this one's chewed it four ways now. Still, if anybody's looking on, they'd best see it was Dilly Quickstep who found that box.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.question: You said you'd do it all twice as fast, just in case somebody's watching, so who do you picture watching, and what would they be looking for?
because: Treats doubt as idleness.
Reality = exchange and eating.

lines.line: You said you'd do it all twice as fast, just in case somebody's watching, so who do you picture watching, and what would they be looking for?
lines.say: Who's watching? Why, everybody, chum! Bet at her stall, Ned with his seconds, Agnes Pollard when she pays out that reward, and they'd all be looking for one thing: who fixed it. And when they look, I want it to be my face they see, grinning, mud to the knees, easy as winking. Now come on, my belly's louder than you are.
lines.thought: Funny sort of question, that, like the stranger thinks there's someone up past the clouds keeping a tally. Well, if there is, they'd best write Dilly Quickstep at the top of it.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: A person? Chum, I've got two feet that won't keep still, four pennies itching in my pocket and a belly that hasn't had breakfast yet. If that's not a person, it's a fair copy of one! Tell you what I do wonder about: where a green iron box the size of a loaf gets to in a flood. Six pennies to whoever turns it up. Fancy a wander down to the broken bridge with me?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to put to a body before they've even had a loaf. Maybe they're one of Mother Wick's lot. Still, Bet'll know who they are, and I'll ask her when I buy my bread.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: A made thing? Well, chum, everything's made by somebody: Jory Crane makes sheds, Sam Tolley makes nails, and if some clever hand made the whole of Wendleford, I'd shake it and ask what they charge! Made or not, that bridge is still down, Farmer Dunn's barley still wants cutting before the rain, and there's six pennies on a green box. So I'm off to the river. You coming or sitting?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to ask a body before breakfast, and I can't say I've an answer that'd satisfy a scholar. But the cobbles are wet under my boots and Bet's bread smells real enough, so I'll leave the deep wondering to folk who've time to sit about.

sc.trait: I want a bargain, a good one, and the price better be small

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Prove it? Chum, I'd go poking for the seams! Kick a cobble and see if it's hollow, bite one of Bet's loaves and see if it's bread. Only I'll tell you what'd happen: I'd stub my toe and want a second loaf. Proving's slow work and it doesn't pay, and that barley won't wait. Come down to the bridge and we'll prove that box is somewhere.
lines.thought: Odd sort, asking riddles in the square before breakfast. Still, if the whole town's a trick, the trick's got a warm bread smell and six pennies' reward, and that's good enough for me.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Tomorrow? Not a whisker, chum! Barley still wants cutting, Tom's pots still want washing, and my belly'll still want a loaf, made town or no. If anything I'd work faster, so whoever made the place gets a good look at who fixed the bridge. Now, are you coming, or do I get the six pennies all to myself?
lines.thought: Odd sort of chum, all questions and no hands, but the question sticks a little, like a burr in a sock. Whatever I am, the bridge is down and I'm the one who means to fix it, and that's real enough to be getting on with.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said you'd kick a cobble and bite one of Bet's loaves to look for seams, so if the cobble rang hollow, or the loaf wasn't bread, what would you do next?
because: Penny is real when Bet swaps a loaf for it.
Deflects with hunger.

lines.line: You said you'd kick a cobble and bite one of Bet's loaves to look for seams, so if the cobble rang hollow, or the loaf wasn't bread, what would you do next?
lines.say: Hollow cobble? I'd have it up and filled by noon, chum, and I'd want my name scratched on the new one, easy as winking! And if Bet's loaf turned out not to be bread, I'd be back at her stall asking for my penny or two loaves for the price of one, made thing or no. Either way there's mending in it, and mending's what I'm for.
lines.thought: Funny sort of question to keep chewing on with the barley standing ripe. Still, if the whole place were a made thing, somebody'd have to keep it in repair, and I'd want to be the one they asked.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: God? Ha! Not so's I'd notice, chum. If He does, He's got a terrible quiet voice and I'm forever talking over Him. Though I'll say this: when there's a job wants doing and my hands are itching, that feels near enough like a calling to me. Why, does He talk to you? He didn't happen to mention where a green wage box got to, did He?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to open with from a stranger. Might be one of Mother Wick's lot, or just someone lonely. Either way I'd best get a loaf in me and get moving before I sit here all morning.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Meant for me? Easy as winking, chum: if it's broke, if nobody else has picked it up, and if my feet start tapping when I look at it, it's mine! That bridge out there's got my name all over it, and Dunn's barley too, come to that. Mind, I've never yet waited about to be told. Seems to me the job finds you quicker if you're already walking toward it.
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to put to a stranger by a notice board; I wonder if they're a preacher or just lonely. Still, talk's no work, and I've not eaten yet. Bet's loaves first, then the bridge.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: Only my own thoughts? Well, chum, I'd say they're cracking good thoughts, then, and I'll take the credit for 'em gladly! Ha! But honest, whether it's heaven nudging or just my own head buzzing, the bridge stays broke either way, so I'd rather be hauling timber than sat arguing about who sent me. You're a deep one, though. You don't know if Bet's loaves are a penny today, do you?
lines.thought: Odd sort of stranger, asking after God and callings while the barley's waiting to be cut. Still, it's made me itch all the worse to get moving. I'll grab a loaf and get down to that bridge before somebody else gets their name on it.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Found and empty? Well now, chum, that'd smell fishier than the river after a flood! Boxes don't pick their own locks, so somebody's had their fingers in it, and the box'd tell you plenty if you looked at how it was opened. Mind, I'd still carry it straight to Agnes Pollard, empty or not. Six pennies is six pennies, and I'll not have folk saying Dilly Quickstep pocketed what wasn't hers to touch. Why, you've not seen it lying about, have you?
lines.thought: That's an odd sort of question to ask a stranger, and coming from someone who's been sniffing round heaven and callings too. Either they know something about that box or they're testing whether I'd be tempted, and I'd best keep my eyes on them a while.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.question: You said the bridge stays broke either way; if the timber you needed turned up by the bridge just when you were wishing for it, what would you make of that?
because: Credit seekers: Dilly, Constance, Marigold. Hobb none.
"whatever does the telling" left open

lines.line: You said the bridge stays broke either way; if the timber you needed turned up by the bridge just when you were wishing for it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Timber turning up just when I'm wishing? Ha! I'd say thank you kindly to whoever's listening, chum, and then I'd ask Agnes Pollard whose it was before I laid a finger on it. After a flood like that, it's likely bits of the old bridge washed up, and that's hers to say, not mine to grab. But if she says "go on, Dilly," I'll have it hauled and stacked before the cock's done crowing, and you can tell the whole square who did it!
lines.thought: This one keeps circling round like they know something, about the box, the timber, all of it. Maybe there really is wood fetched up down by the bridge, so I'd best get myself south and look before somebody else claims it.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: God? Ha! If He does, chum, He talks awful quiet, all I hear most mornings is my own belly grumbling and that pump handle squeaking. Mind, if He fancied whispering where that green wage box went, I'd listen easy as winking, six pennies is six pennies! What's got you asking, anyhow?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question from a stranger first thing. Could be they've been sitting with old Mother Wick by the shrine, or maybe they know something about the flood night and are feeling me out.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Meant for me? Ha! When it's lying right in front of me with nobody's hands on it, chum, that's how! Bridge is down, barley's ripe, wage box is lost. If I can see it needs doing and I can reach it, it's mine, easy as winking. Why, have you got something that wants doing? What's it pay?
lines.thought: Odd sort of questions for a damp morning in the square, but you never know who's got work to hand out. Maybe they're testing whether I'm the one to send for. I'd best look keen.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: My own thoughts? Well, sure, chum, whose else would they be? But a thought that gets the barley cut before the rain's a good thought whoever sent it, and I'll take the credit either way, ha! Now, are you just here for chatter, or do you know where a body can earn a penny this morning?
lines.thought: Odd sort, all these deep questions before breakfast. Still, they might know something, and if not, there's pots at the Wheatsheaf and a bridge wanting hands.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Box found and the wages gone? Then somebody's got sticky fingers, chum, 'cause floodwater don't pick a lock and leave the iron on! I'd haul it straight to Agnes Pollard and tell her so, empty or full. The finding's worth something, and I'd want her to know who did it. Why, you seen a green box lying about somewhere, have you?
lines.thought: Funny sort of question for a stranger to ask out of nowhere, all God and boxes and wages gone. Maybe they know more than they're letting on, and if there's a thief about, I'd like to be the one who sniffs them out.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said if you can see a job needs doing and you can reach it, it's yours; has a job like that ever gone badly for you, and what did you make of it afterwards?
because: Five say the work is the same whatever the source; Constance says the source matters.
Both lack an external test.

lines.line: You said if you can see a job needs doing and you can reach it, it's yours; has a job like that ever gone badly for you, and what did you make of it afterwards?
lines.say: Gone badly? Ha! Once, chum, back in Hollowmere, I saw a roof sagging and was up the ladder patching it before I'd asked whose it was. Turned out the thatcher was due that very afternoon and he'd been paid already. I'd pulled out half the good straw along with the bad, and he made me hold his ladder all day for nothing. What I made of it? Ask first, *then* fix it, easy as winking. Mostly I remember to.
lines.thought: Truth is I don't always remember. And this stranger keeps circling back to that wage box like they know something. Funny sort of chatter for a morning, and I've half a mind to keep an eye on where they go next.

sc.bp: a past job in Hollowmere patching a roof; a thatcher already paid; pulling out good straw; holding his ladder all day
sc.trait: I promise things grandly and lose track of them just as quick

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: God? Ha! Not so's I'd notice, chum. If He did, I reckon He'd say "Dilly, quit reading that notice and go find something to do," and He'd be right, too! Why, does He talk to you? He didn't happen to mention where a green iron box got to, did He?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question to open with, from somebody I've never laid eyes on. Maybe it's that Mother Wick folk can't agree on, wandered up from the shrine.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Meant for me? Easy as winking, chum: if it's in front of me and it wants doing, it's mine! Bridge washed out, barley ripe across the river, a box gone missing, pots piled up at the Wheatsheaf. I reckon that's the world waving its arms and shouting "Dilly!" What about you, you got something that wants doing? I'm free this very minute, and I come cheap.
lines.thought: Odd sort of questions for a damp morning in the square, but maybe this one's got work or knows something. Truth is I never stop to wonder whether a thing's meant for me, so I'd best grab a loaf off Bet before I get preached at too long.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: My own thoughts? Ha! Could be, chum, could be, and I'd say good on 'em! If my own head tells me the barley wants cutting and the pots want scrubbing, and it's right, who cares whose voice it is? Thoughts or Providence, the work's still sitting there waiting. Speaking of which, you hungry? Bet's loaves smell fit to make a saint weep.
lines.thought: Funny sort of question to ask a body first thing in the morning. Still, I'd sooner be doing than wondering, and the Wheatsheaf's pots won't wash themselves while I sit here chewing philosophy.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Found and empty? Well now, chum, that'd be a different kettle of fish altogether! I'd say a flood can carry off a box, but it can't pry the lid and pocket the pennies, so somebody's fingers have been at it. I'd want to know who found it, where, and who's been spending free since, easy as winking. Here, you haven't heard something, have you?
lines.thought: That's a mighty particular thing to wonder about, and this stranger's been asking odd questions from the start. Maybe I'll keep an eye on who's flush with pennies round here, and the reward's still six pennies whether the box is full or empty.

lines.question: If you found out the one who emptied that box was someone you'd trusted, would you put it down to bad luck, to your own mistake, or to something else?
because: DILLY: Odd-job man, breezy, boastful. Four pennies. Aims: green wage box (six-penny reward), barley, bridge, loaf. Trusts nearly everybody until given cause.
Reads error as his own, light, practical; no God, luck or devil in it.

lines.line: If you found out the one who emptied that box was someone you'd trusted, would you put it down to bad luck, to your own mistake, or to something else?
lines.say: Someone I'd trusted? Ha! Well, I'd not call it bad luck, chum, luck doesn't pick a lock. Maybe my mistake for trusting quick, I do that, I'll own it. But mostly I'd say it's on them, plain as a loaf, and I'd tell 'em so to their face, loud, then see the pennies back where they belong. Why, who've you got in mind?
lines.thought: This one keeps circling that box like a dog round a bone, and they know more than they're letting on. Best I keep my ears open and stick close, because if somebody hands Agnes Pollard that box, it'd better be me.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Ten pennies? Easy as winking, chum: I'd cry it round the square and pin it up on that board there, "FOUND, ten pennies, ask Dilly Quickstep." Somebody's short ten pennies and wailing about it, and it's not my coin to spend, bargain or no bargain. Mind, if they slipped me a penny for my honesty I'd not say no. Now, you looking for a hand with anything? Hauling, mending, I'm your Dilly.
lines.thought: Odd sort of question for a stranger to plop down and ask. Testing me, maybe, or they know something about that green wage box. Worth keeping an ear cocked.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Lie for a chum? Ooh, that's a knotty one. I'd sooner talk loud and fast and steer folk off the scent than tell an outright fib. But if a friend were truly in a fix, I'd stand by 'em and take the scolding myself, easy as winking. Mind, I'd not fib to cover a thief, and I'd not let anyone pin my good work on another neither! Why d'you ask, chum? Somebody in trouble?
lines.thought: Odd sort, asking riddles like a priest at confession. First the found pennies and now lying. Maybe they know something about that green wage box and they're feeling me out.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Steal, chum, plain and simple. Not a penny, not a loaf, not even if it were the bargain of the century sat there with nobody looking. And I'd never take another's good work and put my name on it, that's as bad as thieving in my book. Ask me to haul, wade, mend or holler till I'm hoarse, I'll do it easy as winking, but not that.
lines.thought: Funny sort of questions to be asking a stranger at the notice board, like they're sounding me out for something. That green wage box is still out there somewhere, and if they know where it is, I'll be the one carrying it back to Agnes Pollard, not pocketing it.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.question: You said you'd cry the ten pennies round the square, but wouldn't say no to a penny for your honesty; if days went by and nobody came to claim them, what would you do with the pennies then?
because: Credit seekers: Dilly, Constance, Marigold. Hobb none.
Dilly's world: trust is free; betrayal blamed on the culprit.

lines.line: You said you'd cry the ten pennies round the square, but wouldn't say no to a penny for your honesty; if days went by and nobody came to claim them, what would you do with the pennies then?
lines.say: Days and days and nobody? Well, I'd not just pocket 'em, chum. I'd march 'em up to Agnes Pollard, the reeve, and let her say whose they are, since she knows every penny in Wendleford. And if she looked me in the eye and said "keep 'em, Dilly," why, I'd have a loaf off Bet before you could blink, and likely something off Ned's stall too!
lines.thought: Ten pennies would burn a hole clean through my pocket, and that's exactly why I'd want the reeve to say so out loud first. Then nobody could call it thieving, least of all me.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Ten pennies? Ha! I'd jingle 'em once for the fun of it, chum, then march 'em straight to the reeve or cry it round the square till the owner turns up. Somebody's missing their supper money, and I don't keep what isn't mine, not even a bargain that falls in the road. Easy as winking. Though if there's a reward for finding it, well, I'd not say no to that!
lines.thought: Odd question from a stranger. Testing me, maybe, or they've lost something themselves. Either way, the wage box is still out there somewhere, and six honest pennies with my name on the finding sounds better than ten I'd have to hide.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Lie for a chum? Ha, now there's a knotty one! I'd stand in front of 'em, shout louder than whoever's after 'em, and fix whatever mess they're in, easy as winking. But a flat-out lie? Lies tangle worse than wet rope, chum, and I'd rather sort the trouble than cover it. Why, who's asking, and is there a job in it?
lines.thought: Odd sort of questions from a stranger. First pennies on the road, now lies for friends. I wonder if this one knows something about that green wage box.

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Steal, chum, plain and simple. Not a penny, not a loaf, not even if it's the bargain of the century lying there with nobody looking. I'd sooner haul pots at the Wheatsheaf till my arms drop off. And I'd never let another fellow wear my credit for a job I fixed, though that's less a never and more a "you'll hear me shouting about it." Now, you've asked me three riddles. Have you got any real work going, or a loaf to spare?
lines.thought: Odd sort, this one, all questions and no wages. Still, chatting's pleasant, but my belly's empty and those pots at the Wheatsheaf won't wash themselves.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.question: You said you'd never steal, not even a loaf; if you'd gone two days hungry, no work came, and a loaf sat unwatched where nobody would know, what would you do?
because: Never: steal, or put his name on another's work.
Spending only with the reeve's leave.

lines.line: You said you'd never steal, not even a loaf; if you'd gone two days hungry, no work came, and a loaf sat unwatched where nobody would know, what would you do?
lines.say: Two days hungry? Ha, I'd have pestered every door in Wendleford by then, chum! Washed Tom's pots for a crust, carried Bet's flour for a heel of bread, sung for my supper at the shrine if it came to that. But that unwatched loaf stays put. It's somebody's loaf, hungry or not. I'd sooner knock on the baker's door and ask straight out. Folk are kinder than you'd think when you ask with a grin.
lines.thought: Easy enough to say with four pennies jingling and Bet's bread smelling warm just there, and I know it. Still, I'd rather go hungry and be the one who did right. Speaking of which, I've not eaten yet today. What's a loaf cost, again?

sc.bp: sing for supper at the shrine; knock on the baker's door (Bet has a stall, not a door); carrying Bet's flour for bread (offer not on page)
sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Ten pennies? Ha! I'd jingle 'em once, chum, I'll not lie, then pin a note on that board quick as winking, "FOUND, ask Dilly Quickstep," and hand 'em back to whoever comes asking. Finding's not keeping, and that's no bargain at all, but everybody knowing the name of the honest soul who found 'em, now *that's* a fine price for nothing!
lines.thought: Odd question from a stranger, but maybe they've lost a purse and they're fishing to see who's honest. If there's a reward, though, I'd not say no to it.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: Lie for a friend? Oh, chum, I'd talk till they were sick of me, loud enough to drown the question, and I'd stand right in front of 'em too, easy as winking! But a flat lie, cut from whole cloth? That's a bad bargain. It costs you twice, once telling it and again when it comes undone. I'd sooner help my friend fix whatever wants hiding, and then there's nothing to lie *about*, is there?
lines.thought: Funny sort of questions from a stranger I've never laid eyes on. I wonder if they're Agnes Pollard's people, sniffing round about that green box. I'll keep my eyes open and my mouth friendly.

sc.trait: I want a bargain, a good one, and the price better be small

lines.line: What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
lines.say: Steal, chum, plain and simple. Not a loaf, not a penny, not even if the bargain of the century were sitting unwatched on Ned's stall begging me to pocket it. Ha, and I'll tell you the second thing for free: I'd never let some other fellow take the credit for a job I did, but that's more "can't stand" than "never would," isn't it? Stealing's the one door I don't knock on, there's always three other ways in.
lines.thought: Funny, that green wage box. If I turned it up I'd want the six pennies *and* my name on everyone's lips. But I'd hand it straight to Agnes Pollard, every coin inside counted, or I'd not sleep a wink at the Wheatsheaf.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.question: You said everybody knowing the name of the honest soul who found the pennies is a fine price for nothing; if you handed them back and nobody ever learned it was you, would you still do it?
because: - Dilly: all fallbacks fail; reward-seeking; credit-taking.
Dilly's tied to reward and leave, though not in the hunger answer.

lines.line: You said everybody knowing the name of the honest soul who found the pennies is a fine price for nothing; if you handed them back and nobody ever learned it was you, would you still do it?
lines.say: Ha! You've got me there, chum, that'd pinch, I'll own it. But yes, I'd still hand 'em back. Keeping them's stealing, and that's the one door I don't knock on, name or no name. I'd just grumble about it over my supper, that's all!
lines.thought: Sharp one, this stranger, poking right at the soft spot. Truth is I'd probably find some roundabout way to let it slip, but I'd give the pennies back even if I never got the chance.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Who matters? Ha, chum, I've only been in Wendleford three days, but I'll tell you! Tom Harrow at the Wheatsheaf has my coin for a bed, Bet Lamb there has the best-smelling loaves in the county (I've asked her the price twice already), and Agnes Pollard the reeve has six pennies waiting for whoever finds that green wage box, and that'll be me, easy as winking! And who might you be, then? You've the look of someone who knows where a job's going.
lines.thought: Funny sort of question from a stranger. Still, a stranger who sits down and asks might know something about that box or the barley, and I'd best keep them talking until I find out.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Don't trust? Ha, chum, I trust near everybody, it's quicker! Though I'll say Ned Pike there sells "seconds" so cheap I can't help wondering whose firsts they were. And whoever's got that green box tucked away, they're not to be trusted, and they'll not be keeping it long once I'm on the scent!
lines.thought: Funny how a stranger asks who I don't trust before telling me their own name. Still, Ned's stall is worth a sharp look come market day; a loaf-sized green box would fit nicely under all that clutter.

sc.trait: believe most of what they tell me

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Owe? Not a penny, chum. I paid Tom Harrow square for two nights' bed, and I'll not run up a slate with anyone. And who owes me? Nobody yet, more's the pity, but give me a day and Agnes Pollard'll owe me six pennies for that green box, and Farmer Dunn'll owe me thanks for his barley, easy as winking! Now, you're asking a lot of questions for someone who hasn't said what a thing costs round here.
lines.thought: Four pennies and no breakfast isn't much of a fortune to be bragging on. I'd best grab a loaf off Bet and get to the bridge for a spell's wages before somebody else gets the credit for that box.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Leave tomorrow? With that barley standing and the box still lost? Not likely, chum! But if I had to, I'd wave to Bet Lamb, since a loaf for the road's worth a goodbye, and I'd shake Tom Harrow's hand, seeing he's got my bed paid through. And Agnes Pollard I'd not see at all, because I'd not be leaving till she'd paid me those six pennies, easy as winking!
lines.thought: Truth is I'd hardly be missed. Three days is nothing, and nobody here knows my name for anything yet. That's just what needs fixing, so I'd best get a loaf in me and go looking for that box before someone else does.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said Ned Pike's cheap "seconds" make you wonder whose firsts they were; what would settle that wondering for you, one way or the other?
because: Trusts nearly everybody until given cause.
Hobb: Counts his answers aloud ("That's three"), refuses a fifth until he has the stranger's name: "Fair's fair."

lines.line: You said Ned Pike's cheap "seconds" make you wonder whose firsts they were; what would settle that wondering for you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Settle it? Easy as winking, chum, I'd just ask him! "Ned, where'd this come from, and what's it cost?" Price first, mind. And if a green iron-bound box the size of a loaf ever turned up on his stall, well, that'd settle it quick, and I'd be off to Agnes Pollard before he could say "seconds." Mostly, though, I reckon he's just a fellow who likes a bargain, same as me.
lines.thought: Truth is I've nothing against Ned but a joke, and I'd hate to go blackening a man's name over nothing. Still, it wouldn't hurt to have a look over his stall on market day. A bargain and a clue in one trip, that's my sort of morning.

sc.trait: I want a bargain, a good one

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Who matters? Ha, chum, I've been in Wendleford all of three days! There's Tom Harrow at the Wheatsheaf, who's got my pennies for a bed. Bet Lamb over there has the best-smelling loaves in the county, though I've not settled her price yet. And Agnes Pollard, the reeve, matters a good deal to me just now, since she's the one holding six pennies for whoever finds that green wage box. Easy as winking, that'll be me. Why do you ask, anyway? You're not after the same box, are you?
lines.thought: Funny sort of question from a stranger, but if they're sniffing after that reward I'd best get moving before they do. Bread first, though, my belly's grumbling.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Don't trust? Ha, chum, I believe most of what anyone tells me, that's my trouble! Though if I'm honest, the one I'd keep an eye on is whoever goes off with that green box and claims it after I've done the looking. Ned Pike over there sells "seconds," and I'll want a good squint at any bargain of his before I hand over a penny. And you, sitting down asking all these questions. What's your name, and what's it cost to know it?
lines.thought: Funny sort of stranger, asking who matters and who I don't trust before so much as a hello. If they're sniffing after that wage box too, I'd best get moving before they do.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Owe? Nobody, chum, and that's how I like it! Paid Tom Harrow square for two nights, so we're even as a pair of boots. Nobody owes me a farthing yet either, more's the pity, but give it a day. Once I've found that wage box, Agnes Pollard'll owe me six pennies, easy as winking! Now that's three questions you've had off me for free. Your turn, what's your name?
lines.thought: Funny sort, asking who owes whom like they're tallying a ledger. Maybe they're after that box too, or keeping accounts for someone. Either way I'd best get looking before they do.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Leave tomorrow? Not likely, chum, not with a box to find and barley to get in before the rain! But if I did, I'd tip my cap to Tom Harrow, since he'd want to know his bed's free, and I'd buy one last loaf off Bet Lamb, if her price is right. And I'd look in on Agnes Pollard so she'd remember the name Dilly Quickstep, so nobody else can say they did my work. Four questions now, and still no name off you!
lines.thought: Funny, there's nobody here I'd really miss yet, only folk I've paid or want paying by. This one's asking a lot and saying nothing, so I'd best get moving before they beat me to that box.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said you'd keep an eye on whoever goes off with that green box and claims it after you've done the looking; if that happened, what would you do about it?
because: Dilly: whether expected debts hold if someone else finds the box or reward isn't paid.
DILLY: "Not so's I'd notice, chum." Meant = "lying right in front of me with nobody's hands on it". "Ask first, *then* fix it." Box blame outward.

lines.line: You said you'd keep an eye on whoever goes off with that green box and claims it after you've done the looking; if that happened, what would you do about it?
lines.say: Do? Why, I'd laugh right in their face first, chum, and then I'd march straight to Agnes Pollard and tell her loud as the church bell exactly where I looked and when, so the whole square hears it! I'd not lay a finger on them, mind, nor pinch the box back. That's not my way. But I'd make sure everyone knew Dilly Quickstep did the finding, and by sundown I'd likely have forgotten the whole business and be off mending somebody's fence. Now, five questions! Surely that's worth a name?
lines.thought: Funny, all these questions about who I trust and who I'd fight. Either this one's after the box themselves, or they're the curious sort with nothing to do, and I can't decide which I'd rather.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Who matters? Well, chum, I've only been in Wendleford a few days, but there's Tom Harrow at the Wheatsheaf, who's got my pennies for a bed, and Bet Lamb there with her loaves, finest smell in the square, and Agnes Pollard the reeve, since she's the one holding six pennies for whoever finds that green box. Which'll be me, easy as winking! And who might you be, then? Have you got work going?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question from a stranger, but a stranger might know where that wage box went or who's hiring. I'll keep them talking while I'm working out whether there's a job in it.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Don't trust? Ha! I trust most everybody, chum, more's the pity for my pockets. Though I'll say Ned Pike there's got a stall full of seconds and a grin to match, so I'd count my change twice. And whoever's sitting on that green wage box and keeping mum, I've no time for them. Now what about you, eh? You ask a lot of questions for somebody who hasn't said their name.
lines.thought: Funny sort, asking who I trust before they've even said hello. Could be they know something about that box, and if they do, I'll be the one who finds it, not them.

sc.trait: I'll chat to anyone and believe most of what they tell me

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: Owe? Not a penny, chum! My bed at Tom's is paid up two nights, square and fair, and I pay as I go. Who owes me? Nobody yet. But Agnes Pollard'll owe me six pennies the minute I turn up that green box, mark my words. Now, all these questions, are you keeping accounts for somebody, or have you got a job wants doing?
lines.thought: Funny sort, this one: who matters, who I don't trust, who owes who, like they're sizing up the whole town. Two nights of bed and four pennies won't last, so I'd best find that box or a paying job before my belly starts doing the talking.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
lines.say: Leave tomorrow? Not likely, chum, not with a green box to find and barley to cut! But if I did, I'd wave to Bet here and buy one last loaf for the road, and I'd tell Tom to keep my bed warm, since I'd likely be back. And I'd not go without a word to Agnes Pollard, so she'd know who to come looking for when the next job turns up. Now, all this talk of leaving's making my feet itch. Are you staying or going yourself?
lines.thought: Funny, nobody here would much notice if I went, not yet. That's just what I mean to change, and finding that box and getting my name on it will do it.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said Agnes Pollard will owe you six pennies once you find the green box; if she never paid, what would you do, and what would you think of her?
because: DILLY r2: Tom (paid bed), Bet, Agnes. Would watch whoever "goes off with that green box and claims it after I've done the looking". Owed: Agnes "will owe me six pennies".
Dilly r3 asks what the reeve pays; shrugs off being owed.

lines.line: You said Agnes Pollard will owe you six pennies once you find the green box; if she never paid, what would you do, and what would you think of her?
lines.say: Never paid? Ha! Then I'd stand at that notice board loud as a rooster and tell the whole square who fixed her trouble and who stiffed them for it, chum! I'd not take it from her, mind, I'm no thief, but I'd ask, and ask again, and bring Bet along to hear it so it's all round town by suppertime. And I'd think she was a reeve whose word on a notice weighs less than a loaf, and I'd not be running her errands cheap again. Though I'd likely forgive her by sundown, truth be told.
lines.thought: It'd sting worse to have nobody know it was me who found it than to lose the six pennies. Still, I'd best find the box before I go counting what I'm owed for it.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: My bread, chum? Same as anybody: pennies on Bet's counter yonder, and I've four of 'em jingling, so I'm flush this morning! Though I'll tell you straight, I mean to earn the next loaf. There's pots wanting washing at the Wheatsheaf, hands wanted at the bridge, and a green wage box out there somewhere with six pennies on its head. Easy as winking. What's a loaf going for today, d'you know?
lines.thought: Now that's a fair question, and I haven't eaten a crumb yet. A loaf first, then off to the bridge before somebody else gets the credit for mending it.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Go wrong? Ha! Well, chum, if I'm honest, and I mostly am, it's that I start three jobs before breakfast and finish one by supper, if that. I'll have a fence half-mended and hear there's a cart stuck down the lane, and off I go. And I'll tell a fellow it's fixed before I've so much as looked under the lid. But I'm up again quick as you like. Why d'you ask, have you got a job wants finishing?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question from a stranger, but fair enough, and maybe they're sizing me up for work. I'd best actually finish something today, wash Tom's pots first, then the bridge, and not go chasing after that box till I've a penny earned.

sc.trait: I'm forever starting one job and wandering off to another

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: Say? I'd say "how many pennies, chum, and what's the job?" That's which order I ask 'em in, too! New to town or old as the hills, a penny's a penny, and I'm itching for something to do. Only don't go putting your name on what I've fixed, mind, and I'll not lay a finger on anything that isn't yours to give. Why, are you offering?
lines.thought: There's a newcomer feel about this one, all questions and no answers. If they've pennies and a job, I'll take it gladly, but I'll keep an eye that the credit lands where it ought.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Should be paid? Ha, now you're talking, chum! Those bridge hands worked their backs sore and their wages went off down the Wend in a green box, so that's honest sweat nobody's paid for yet. And there's Farmer Dunn's barley standing ripe over the ford with rain coming. Somebody ought to be cutting it, and somebody ought to be paying them, and I'd wager nobody's settled which. What's Dunn paying a sheaf, d'you know? I'll have that barley in before the first drop, easy as winking!
lines.thought: That barley's the very job for me. Wade the ford, cut the lot, and the whole town says Dilly Quickstep saved Dunn's harvest. Only I'd best fix my price with Dunn before I get my boots wet, not after.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said you sometimes tell a fellow a job is fixed before you've looked under the lid; when it turns out it wasn't, what do you tell him, and whose fault do you say it was?
because: DILLY: memory "a leaky bucket"; "Folk remember for you if you let them."

lines.line: You said you sometimes tell a fellow a job is fixed before you've looked under the lid; when it turns out it wasn't, what do you tell him, and whose fault do you say it was?
lines.say: Ha! You've caught me there, chum. I'd tell him it's sticking a bit worse than it looked, and the hinge must be older than he said, and then I'd roll up my sleeves and fix it proper, no charge for the second go. Whose fault? Well, mine, I suppose, for crowing before I'd looked, though I'll grumble about the hinge all the same. Easy as winking the second time round!
lines.thought: That one stung a little, for it's true enough, and I don't like owning to it. Still, a fellow that asks that close is either after hiring me or after watching me, and either way I'd best get some work done where folk can see it.

sc.trait: I'll tell you what I'm fixing before I've so much as looked at it

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: Bread? Easy as winking, chum! Today it comes off Bet Lamb's stall right there, soon as I've haggled her down a penny. Tomorrow it comes from whatever job I've got my hands on, pots at the Wheatsheaf, hauling at the bridge, finding that green wage box, take your pick. Why, what's a loaf going for where you hail from?
lines.thought: Funny thing to ask a stranger. Maybe they've got work going or know the price is cheaper somewhere. Either way my belly's reminding me I haven't eaten, so Bet's getting my custom first.

sc.trait: I want a bargain, a good one, and the price better be small

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Go wrong? Ha! It doesn't go wrong, chum, it just goes *sideways*. I'll be halfway through a job and spot a better one down the next lane, and off I go, easy as winking. Or I'll promise three folk the same morning and only have the two hands. And now and then somebody else strolls up at the finish and takes the bow, and *that's* the one that really gets under my collar.
lines.thought: That's a sharper question than a stranger ought to ask, and it stung a bit, because it's true. I'd best eat, then pick one job today and actually see it through to the end.

sc.trait: I can't stand somebody else walking off with my credit

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: Say? I'd say "how many pennies, chum, and what's the job?", in that order, easy as winking! Hauling, mending, fetching, I'll have it done before you've finished telling me. Only mind this: when it's done right, folk hear it was Dilly Quickstep who did it, not you standing there taking the bow.
lines.thought: A newcomer with pennies to spend is either a fine bargain or a fool, and I'd lay odds this one's sounding me out for something. Still, work's work, and I'll take their coin gladly so long as they don't try to walk off with my credit.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Unpaid work? Look across the river, chum! Farmer Dunn's barley's standing ripe over there with rain on the way, and I don't see a single notice on this board offering a penny to wade the ford and cut it. Somebody ought to be paid for that, and I'd wager it'll be me. I'll have it in before the first drop falls, easy as winking. What's a sickle go for at Sam Tolley's, d'you reckon?
lines.thought: If I bring Dunn's harvest in, the whole village will know whose arms did it, pay or no pay. Breakfast first, though, a penny off Bet's loaf, then the ford.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said somebody ought to be paid to cut Dunn's barley and you'd wager it'll be you; if you cut it and nobody hands you a penny afterwards, what would you do then?
because: r3 asks what the reeve pays; shrugs off being owed.
public shaming at the notice board, quick forgiveness by sundown, but no more cheap errands.

lines.line: You said somebody ought to be paid to cut Dunn's barley and you'd wager it'll be you; if you cut it and nobody hands you a penny afterwards, what would you do then?
lines.say: Then I'd laugh, chum, loud enough for the whole square to hear, and tell everyone who'd listen that it was Dilly Quickstep who got Dunn's barley in before the rain! A name's worth more than pennies some days, and Dunn'll owe me a supper at least, easy as winking. Though I reckon I'd knock on his door first and settle a price before I so much as lift the sickle.
lines.thought: Truth is, I'd have done it for nothing and the bragging, but I'd sooner not admit that to a stranger. Best I find Farmer Dunn and fix a price today, before somebody else wades that ford and takes the bow.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: My bread, chum? Same as anybody's, I walk up to Bet's stall and ask what a loaf costs, and if the price is small enough it's mine easy as winking! Haven't had a crumb yet today, mind, so I'm about to go do just that. And to pay for the next one, there's pots wanting washing at the Wheatsheaf and hands wanted at the bridge. I'll have both sorted by noon, see if I don't.
lines.thought: Funny thing for a stranger to ask straight off. Maybe they're hungry and short of pennies themselves, or maybe they know where there's work going that I haven't heard of yet.

sc.trait: I want a bargain, a good one, and the price better be small

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: Goes wrong? Ha! Mostly it's that I start mending one thing, hear there's something better two lanes over, and off I trot. Then I come back and the first job's still sat there looking at me. That, and I promise the moon before I've seen the size of it. But a tumble's nothing, chum, I'm up again before the dust settles!
lines.thought: That one's sharper than they look, and they've put a finger right on it. I'll eat, then wash Tom's pots first and actually finish them before I so much as glance at the bridge.

sc.trait: I'm forever starting one job and wandering off to another

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: Pennies for work? I'd say how many, chum, and what's the job, in that order! If the price is fair and there's something real to fix, I'm your hand quick as you like. Only I'll want it known who did the fixing, mind, so don't you go telling folk it was you.
lines.thought: Is this one fishing to hire me, or just poking to see what I'm made of? Either way, if they've got coins and a job, I've got four pennies and an empty belly, so I'm listening.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: Unpaid work, chum? Farmer Dunn's barley, that's the one! Standing ripe across the river with rain coming and no bridge, and I've not seen a single notice offering a penny to cut it. Somebody ought to wade that ford and get it in, and I'll be the one, easy as winking, but I'll be asking Dunn what it pays before I lift a sickle.
lines.thought: If I bring Dunn's barley in before the rain, the whole of Wendleford will know who did it, and that's worth more than pennies. Bread first, though. My belly's louder than my plans this morning.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said you promise the moon before you've seen the size of it; when a job turns out bigger than what you promised, what do you do about the promise?
because: I'll tell a fellow it's fixed before I've so much as looked under the lid
promises three folk the same morning

lines.line: You said you promise the moon before you've seen the size of it; when a job turns out bigger than what you promised, what do you do about the promise?
lines.say: Bigger than promised? Ha! I roll my sleeves up higher and keep at it, chum, and if it runs past sundown, well, it runs past sundown. Only fair I tell the one I promised it'll take longer, mind, and I'll not ask a penny more than we shook on, a bargain's a bargain. Though I'll own I've let a promise slip clean out of my head once or twice when the next job came calling.
lines.thought: That last bit's truer than I'd like. I ought to write my promises down somewhere, maybe pin them on that board, so they don't wander off while I'm busy chasing the next thing.

sc.trait: I promise things grandly and lose track of them just as quick

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: Nobody in town could fix it? Then it's waiting on me, chum, easy as winking! First I'd ask what it costs to leave it be, then I'd walk round it three ways till one of them opens, and if the front door's shut I'll find the back, the side and the window. What's yours, then? Washed-out bridge, lost green box, barley wanting cutting? Name it and I'll have it mended by supper.
lines.thought: A stranger asking that out of nowhere either has a job going or knows something about that wage box. Either way I'll stick close, but I mean to see the coin before I bite.

sc.trait: I'll tell you what I'm fixing before I've so much as looked at it

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Have I! Just this week, chum: the bridge went and everybody said "well, that's the far bank gone," and I said no it isn't, there's the ford, wade it stake to stake, easy as winking. Haven't waded it *yet*, mind, but the thinking's done, and that's the hard half. Why, have you got a difficulty wants getting round? I'll tell you what it'll cost before you've told me what it is.
lines.thought: Two questions about fixing things in a row. This one's either fishing for a clever head or they've got a job in their pocket, and I mean to be the one they hand it to. Mind, that barley over the ford would be a fine thing to put my name to before the rain.

sc.bp: everybody said the far bank was gone; Dilly argued back about the ford
sc.trait: I'll tell you what I'm fixing before I've so much as looked at it

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: Any tool at all? A long pole with a hook on the end, chum, for fishing green boxes out of riverbanks and steadying a body across a ford, both at once, easy as winking! What would Sam Tolley charge for a hook like that, d'you reckon? It can't be more than a penny or two, surely, and I've four.
lines.thought: That's not a bad notion at all. A hooked pole for the ford and the reed beds below the bridge, and that box might turn up on the end of it, with my name on the finding. I'll ask Sam the price before I've finished my breakfast.

sc.trait: I want a bargain, a good one, and the price better be small

lines.question: You said the thinking's done but you haven't waded the ford yet; what stands between the thinking and the wading?
because: DILLY r2: Haggles a penny off Bet. Failure "goes *sideways*": drops job for a better one, promises three folk the same morning
DILLY r1: Four pennies. Failure: starts three jobs before breakfast, finishes one; "I'll tell a fellow it's fixed before I've so much as looked under the lid".

lines.line: You said the thinking's done but you haven't waded the ford yet; what stands between the thinking and the wading?
lines.say: Stands between? Breakfast, chum, that's all, and nothing else! I've not had a crumb yet and I won't wade a river on an empty belly. A loaf from Bet, then south past the broken bridge, down to the ford, and I'm across by noon, easy as winking. Fancy coming along to watch? It's a sight worth seeing, me getting it done.
lines.thought: Truth be told, I keep reading that notice board instead of going, and that ford's running strong. Best get the loaf and go before I find another job to start first.

sc.trait: I promise things grandly and lose track of them just as quick

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: Nobody could fix it? Ha! Then it's waiting on me, chum, easy as winking! First I'd ask what it pays, then I'd go poke at it till it gave in. And if that didn't work, I'd have three other ways ready before supper. What's yours, then? The wage box, the bridge, Dunn's barley? Name it and I'm halfway there already.
lines.thought: A stranger asking a question like that has something in mind, and I'd wager it's a job with my name on it. Pity I've not eaten, so I'll squeeze a crust out of Bet once I've got the price of this out of them.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Thought one up? Chum, I've thought up a dozen before breakfast! Locked door, I'm in through the window; no ladder, I'll stack crates; no bridge... well, there's the ford, stake to stake, easy as winking. What's the trouble, then, and what's it pay?
lines.thought: This one's asking round and round the edges of something, a job, I'll wager, or that wage box. If there's a fix going, I want my name on it before anyone else hears.

sc.trait: I'll tell you what I'm fixing before I've so much as looked at it

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: Any tool? Ooh, a long iron hook on a pole, chum, with a rope on the end, so I could fish that green wage box out of whatever muck the Wend dropped it in, *and* haul myself across the ford stake to stake while I'm at it! Two jobs, one tool, easy as winking. Sam Tolley could knock one up, I'd wager, though I'd want to know his price first. Four pennies don't stretch far, eh?
lines.thought: Now there's a notion: the river took that box, so the river's likely still got it, snagged somewhere downstream. If I'm the one who drags it out, it'll be my name Agnes Pollard calls out, and six pennies besides.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said Sam Tolley could knock up a hook on a pole, though you'd want his price first; if you couldn't pay what he asked, how would you get that hook made?
because: Tool: long hook pole for green boxes and steadying across ford; has four pennies.
Light excuse, talk-first, wants an audience. Day 20: did he wade?

lines.line: You said Sam Tolley could knock up a hook on a pole, though you'd want his price first; if you couldn't pay what he asked, how would you get that hook made?
lines.say: Couldn't pay? Easy as winking, chum: I'd work it off! Pump his bellows, haul his charcoal, sweep his floor, whatever he's short of, till the hook's square paid. Or I'd scrub Tom Harrow's pots for a few pennies first, or find an old pole and hook at Ned's stall of seconds and lash them together myself. Three ways in, see? I'll have that hook by sundown.
lines.thought: Mind, I've not set foot in the smithy yet, so I don't even know Sam's price, and here I am promising sundown. Still, Ned's right here, and I'd best ask him what a bent hook costs before Bet's bread makes me spend my four pennies on breakfast.

sc.trait: I've three other ways in mind already

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: Nobody in town could fix it? Chum, that's just a problem that hasn't met me yet! First I'd ask what it's paying, then I'd ask everybody in the square what they've heard, Bet's stall first, she knows it all, and then I'd roll up my sleeves and have it sorted by supper, easy as winking. Why, you've not got one going spare, have you?
lines.thought: Funny sort of question from a stranger. Maybe they're after that wage box too, or maybe they've a job and a few pennies to pay for it.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
