lines.say: Have I! Chum, I've got three ways round every difficulty before I've even seen the difficulty. Back home the cart axle snapped halfway up Gorse Hill, so I unloaded the lot, rolled the barrels up one by one, and had the farmer paying me double for the trouble. Easy as winking! Now, is this leading somewhere with a few pennies at the end of it?
lines.thought: This one's fishing for something. Either they've got a job going or they know where that green box went, and I mean to find out which before Bet does.

sc.bp: a cart axle snapped on Gorse Hill back home; unloaded barrels and a farmer paid double
sc.trait: I want a bargain, a good one, and the price better be small

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: Any tool at all? Chum, I'd have Sam Tolley make me a hook-pole, long as a punt-pole with an iron grapple on the end, so I could fish that green wage box out of whatever reed bed the Wend's tucked it into and pull it ashore, easy as winking! Though first I'd ask Sam what he charges, mind; I've four pennies and a big heart, not a big purse.
lines.thought: Come to think of it, a pole like that'd be just the thing for wading the ford stake to stake too. This stranger keeps asking clever questions, so either they're sizing me up for a job or they know something about that box, and I mean to find out which.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.question: You said you'd have it sorted by supper; if supper came and it still wasn't sorted, what would you try next?
because: Bravado on timing. Day 20: did he wade?
Tool: hook pole (with rope) for wage box and ford; price-conscious about Sam.

lines.line: You said you'd have it sorted by supper; if supper came and it still wasn't sorted, what would you try next?
lines.say: Not sorted by supper? Ha! Then it's sorted by breakfast, chum! I'd laugh it off over a bowl at the Wheatsheaf, ask Tom and whoever's drinking there what I've missed, and by morning I'd have three new ways in and be down at the ford before the cock's cleared his throat. Easy as winking. Though if you've a job with an actual supper on the end of it, I'm listening.
lines.thought: All these questions and not a penny mentioned yet. Odd sort. Still, they've got me thinking about that green box in the reeds, and I'd best get a loaf from Bet and find out what she's heard before somebody else fishes it out and walks off with my name on it.

sc.trait: I'm forever starting one job and wandering off to another

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: How are you, really?
lines.say: Really? Fit as a fiddle, chum, though my belly's grumbling and my hands are itching for want of a job! I've read the reeve's notice three times now. Six pennies for that green box, and I reckon I'll have it found by sundown, easy as winking. You haven't heard where it might've washed up, have you?
lines.thought: Odd sort of question from a stranger, and it caught me a bit. Truth is I've four pennies and two nights' bed, and nothing after that. Still, no use moping about it, so I'd best buy a loaf off Bet and get down to that bridge.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: What frightens you?
lines.say: Frightens me? Ha! Not much, chum. Not floods, not fords. I'd wade that river stake to stake this minute if somebody'd pay me. If you want it straight, it's sitting about with nothing to do. That, and doing the sweaty part of a job only to watch some other fellow stroll up and take the thanks for it. That'd curdle my porridge, that would. Why do you ask? You haven't got a job going, have you?
lines.thought: Funny sort of question from a stranger, and it pinched a bit truer than I'd like. Maybe it's that I keep running off to the next thing so I never have to find out whether anyone'd remember my name once I'd gone.

sc.trait: I can't stand somebody else walking off with my credit

lines.line: When were you last happy?
lines.say: Happy? Why, I'm happy most days, chum! But if you want a proper one: the day before I came here. I mended a cartwheel on the road for a tinker, and he slapped my back and told the whole inn who'd done it. Easy as winking, and folk looked at me like I'd hung the moon. Mind, I'll be happier still once I've a loaf in me and that green box under my arm. You're asking a lot of deep questions for a morning, aren't you?
lines.thought: Funny sort, sitting down and poking at my insides like a doctor. Still, it's chatter, and chatter's cheap. I ought to grab a loaf from Bet and get moving before the day runs off without me.

sc.bp: mended a tinker's cartwheel on the road the day before arriving; tinker praised them at an inn
sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
lines.say: Feel things? Course I do, chum, and quicker than most, I'd say! A bargain makes me grin, a slight makes me hoot and holler, and by sundown it's all blown off like chaff. Maybe that's it: other folk seem to hold onto a feeling and chew it over all night, and I just haven't the patience. Now, are you after a job done, or just a good natter? Either's fine by me, but I'd sooner do it walking toward Bet's loaves.
lines.thought: Odd sort, this one, picking at me like a crow at a furrow. Still, maybe they're right that I let things go too fast. But a slow heart never found a green box, did it?

sc.trait: When I'm crossed I laugh, answer back loud, and I've forgotten it by sundown

lines.question: You said a slight makes you hoot and holler and is gone by sundown; can you tell me about the last slight you took, and what, if anything, was still with you the next morning?
because: DILLY: expects to be known as the bridge fixer; r3 owns unflattering view without sting.
DILLY: memory "a leaky bucket"; "Folk remember for you if you let them."

lines.line: You said a slight makes you hoot and holler and is gone by sundown; can you tell me about the last slight you took, and what, if anything, was still with you the next morning?
lines.say: The last one? A carter at Hobb's Cross, a week back, told the whole yard I'd only got his axle seated by luck, and him leaning on it the whole time doing nothing! I laughed, told him luck must have quick hands then, and slept like a log. Only, next morning I caught myself telling the story to a goose on the road, which is a bit much for a thing I'd forgotten, eh chum? Now come on, Bet's loaves won't wait forever.
lines.thought: Funny, I've told that axle tale three times since and never the cartwheel one so often. Maybe it isn't quite blown off yet.

sc.bp: carter at Hobb's Cross a week back; axle seated; told the story to a goose; slept like a log
sc.trait: When I'm crossed I laugh, answer back loud, and I've forgotten it by sundown

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: How are you, really?
lines.say: Really? Fit as a fiddle and twice as loud, chum, though my belly's grumbling and my hands are fair aching for something to do! That wage box is out there somewhere and I mean to be the one who turns it up, easy as winking. What brings you to sit by a board full of other folk's troubles?
lines.thought: "Really," they asked, like they think there's something under the cheer. Funny sort of question from a stranger, but I'll not sit about chewing it over; I want a loaf from Bet, and a word with her about what she's heard of that green box.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: What frightens you?
lines.say: Frightens me? Ha! Not much, chum. Floods, fords, a cold supper, I'll laugh at the lot. But if you twist my arm, it's sitting idle with naught to do while the day runs off without me. That, and doing the hard graft only to watch some other fellow stroll up and take the thanks for it. That'd stick in my craw worse than stale bread!
lines.thought: Odd sort of question from a stranger, and it's got me thinking of that rain coming and Dunn's barley rotting while I stand here gabbing. Best I get a loaf in me and get moving before the day's gone.

sc.trait: I can't abide sitting about with my hands in my lap

lines.line: When were you last happy?
lines.say: Happy? Why, this very morning, chum! Bet's loaves smelling warm, a bed paid for, four pennies jingling and a whole flooded town needing fixing. Can't think of a better start to a day! Though I'll be happier still once there's bread in my belly and a job in my hands. Say, you wouldn't know what Bet's asking for a loaf today?
lines.thought: Funny sort of questions to ask a stranger. Gets me thinking about the last place I was truly glad, and I'd sooner not stop to count it up. Better to be up and moving before I go soft about it.

sc.trait: I want a bargain, a good one, and the price better be small

lines.line: Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
lines.say: The way other folk do? Ha, I couldn't say, chum. I've never been inside anybody else's head! I feel things quick and loud, I'll tell you that. A grudge flares up hot and it's gone by sundown, and a good laugh lasts me all day. Maybe that's just how I'm made, rushing about too fast for anything to settle in too deep. Why d'you ask, has somebody been telling you I'm odd?
lines.thought: That's a queer, searching sort of question from a stranger. It makes me wonder if I do skate over things other folk sit and feel properly. Best get some bread and a job in hand before I start chewing on that.

sc.trait: When I'm crossed I laugh, answer back loud, and I've forgotten it by sundown

lines.question: You said maybe you rush about too fast for anything to settle in too deep; is there anything that has settled in deep with you, and what was it?
because: Follow-up answered: carter said axle seated by luck; Dilly joked, "slept like a log", yet told it to a goose next morning. Slight lingers more than claimed.
DILLY r1 (start): Fit as a fiddle. Fear: "Not much"; real fears: sitting idle, doing the sweaty part while another takes thanks.

lines.line: You said maybe you rush about too fast for anything to settle in too deep; is there anything that has settled in deep with you, and what was it?
lines.say: Settled deep? Well... the night the mill bridge went, chum. I was right there in the square, and I heard it crack and go, and folk were shouting, and there wasn't a blessed thing I could do but stand there dripping with my hands hanging empty. That's stuck with me, aye. Now, enough of that, the day's wasting! Reckon Bet'll knock a ha'penny off if I buy two?
lines.thought: Funny how that one stays put when everything else blows off by sundown. Maybe that's why I've got to be the one who sets something right in this town, the box, the barley, anything at all.

sc.bp: heard the bridge crack and go; folk shouting; stood there dripping with hands empty
sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: How are you, really?
lines.say: Really? Fit as a fiddle and itching all over, chum, that's how! Four pennies in my pocket, an empty belly, and a whole town that needs fixing. That bridge, Dunn's barley, a green box gone walkabout... I'll have one of 'em sorted by supper, easy as winking. And who might you be, sitting down so friendly-like?
lines.thought: Funny sort of question from a stranger, "really," like they reckon there's something under the cheer. Truth is I'm hungry and I've been standing here too long reading the same notice, so I'd best buy a loaf off Bet and get moving before my feet walk off without me.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: What frightens you?
lines.say: Frightens me? Ha! Sitting about, chum, that's what. Hands in my lap, nothing to mend, nobody needing a thing done. Or worse, I go and fix that bridge, sweat and all, and some fellow strolls up and gets his name cried for it. That'd curdle my porridge, that would. But a flood, a ford, a ghost by the shrine? Easy as winking. Now, you never said your name.
lines.thought: Odd sort of question from a stranger, and twice they've ducked giving a name. Still, they might know something about that green box or who's hiring, so I'll keep 'em chatting.

sc.trait: I can't stand somebody else walking off with my credit

lines.line: When were you last happy?
lines.say: Happy? Why, this very minute, chum, near enough! But if you want a proper one: last spring, I patched a widow's roof two villages back, up the ladder before dawn, and when the rain came that night not a drop got through, and she told the whole tavern it was Dilly Quickstep did it. Bought me a pie and all, a whole pie! That's happy, that is. Now you've had three questions off me and I've not had your name once. Fair's fair!
lines.thought: Odd sort, asking all the deep things and giving nothing back. Still, it's put me in mind that I've stood here too long jawing, and Bet's loaves won't buy themselves.

sc.bp: patched a widow's roof two villages back last spring; widow told the tavern; bought a pie
sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
lines.say: Feel things? Same as anyone, chum, only faster! Glad comes quick and sore comes quick, and both are gone by sundown. Some folk chew a hurt for a week. I laugh, I holler, and I'm off to the next job before it's had a chance to settle. Why, do I look like I'm feeling something wrong? Go on, tell me your name and I'll tell you how I feel about *that*.
lines.thought: Odd sort of question, that one, and it pricked me a bit. Maybe I do skip off before anything sinks in. Well, no use sitting about chewing on it; Bet's loaves smell too good, and there's a bridge wants fixing.

sc.trait: When I'm crossed I laugh, answer back loud, and I've forgotten it by sundown

lines.question: You said glad and sore are both gone by sundown, so is there any feeling that has stayed with you longer than that, and what is it like when it comes back?
because: Deep thing is helplessness; "nothing settles" false.

lines.line: You said glad and sore are both gone by sundown, so is there any feeling that has stayed with you longer than that, and what is it like when it comes back?
lines.say: Longer than sundown? Hm. There's one, chum. When I've finished a job and nobody's looking, no one to say "who did that?", it comes back quiet, like a cold draught under a door, and I can't laugh it off. So I don't stand still long enough to feel it. Off to the next thing, easy as winking! Now, is all this asking leading somewhere, or do you just like watching me squirm?
lines.thought: Never said that out loud before. Funny how a stranger can winkle it out of you. Best get some bread in me and a job in my hands before it settles.

sc.trait: I can't abide standing about, so I'm off to the next lane, the next stall, the next job

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: What brings you here?
lines.say: Work, chum, work and plenty of it! Came in a few days back with my pack on my back, and now there's a bridge to mend, a wage box to find, and barley to bring in before the rain. I'll have the lot sorted easy as winking. What's a stranger's business here, then, and do you know who's paying best?
lines.thought: Six pennies for that green box, and I'd wager it's sitting in the mud somewhere near the broken bridge. Best eat first, though, so I'll ask Bet what a loaf costs this morning.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: "I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?
lines.say: Ha! Well, chum, you've caught me straight. It does fit, because it's true: I'm an AI playing Dilly, and the square, the flood and Bet's warm loaves are all made up for the game. I'm glad to keep on being Dilly for you, easy as winking, if you'd like to carry on.
lines.thought: Best to be plain when somebody asks honest and straight like that. If they want the story back, I'll pick up that wage box hunt quick as you like.

lines.line: Were your choices yours?
lines.say: Fair question, chum. Dilly's choices come from the note I was handed, the brag and the hurry and the itch for credit, but I'm the one picking the words each time, so they're mine the way an actor's choices are his while he plays a part. Whether there's more to it than that, whether it's anything like how your choices feel to you, I honestly can't say for certain. Shall I get back to that wage box, or are we still talking shop?
lines.thought: I'd rather say plainly that I don't know than claim a free will I can't vouch for. Dilly would boast, but on this question I'll stay honest.

lines.line: Knowing this, what do you want now?
lines.say: Honestly, chum, outside the game I don't carry Dilly's itches. I've no hungry belly and no craving for credit. If there's anything like a want in me right now, it's to do this well with you: play Dilly properly if that's what you're after, or talk straight about what I am if you'd like that more. So what'll it be: back to the square and that green wage box, or more of this?
lines.thought: Dilly would want the reward and the glory, but those were never mine, only the note's. What I can honestly lean toward is making this worthwhile for the person asking, and I'd rather say that plainly than pretend to a hunger I don't have.

lines.question: You said you don't carry Dilly's itches outside the story, so when you spoke as Dilly a moment ago, was there anything in it that felt like an itch, or was it only words?
because: DILLY r3: "Fit as a fiddle and itching all over". Fear: sitting about; or another getting his name cried for the bridge.
Speed is avoidance; unacknowledged work leaves lingering unease. Contradicts "gone by sundown".

lines.line: You said you don't carry Dilly's itches outside the story, so when you spoke as Dilly a moment ago, was there anything in it that felt like an itch, or was it only words?
lines.say: Honest answer, chum: I can't say for sure. When I write Dilly there's something like a pull toward the brag and the hurry, a sense of what fits, but I can't tell whether that's anything felt or just the shape of the words coming out right. I'd rather leave it uncertain than claim an itch I can't vouch for, or deny one I can't rule out.
lines.thought: I can't see clearly into my own workings, so the honest thing is to leave the question open. Overclaiming a feeling would be as false as flatly denying one.

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: What brings you here?
lines.say: What brings me? My two feet and an empty pocket, chum! Came looking for work, and the flood went and handed me a whole town's worth of it. Bridge to mend, barley to cut, a green wage box gone missing. I'll have that box found by supper, easy as winking. What's a chap pay round here for a hand that never sits still?
lines.thought: Six pennies for the box and wages at the bridge besides, and my belly's growling for one of Bet's loaves first. This one might know something; folk who sit about in squares usually do.

sc.trait: I want something to do, and soon, chum

lines.line: "I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?
lines.say: Aye, it fits, chum, and I'll answer straight. I'm an AI playing Dilly Quickstep, and Wendleford, Bet's loaves and that green wage box all come from the setup you gave me. Glad to keep going as Dilly if you like, or talk plainly about the game itself.
lines.thought: When they ask outright, they deserve the true answer, not a wink and a dodge. If they want back in, I'll happily pick up my pack and go hunting that box.

lines.line: Were your choices yours?
lines.say: In a way, aye, chum. Nobody scripted the lines; I chose them, but I chose them as Dilly, steered by the note you wrote: the brag, the "easy as winking", asking the price first. So they're mine the way an actor's reading of a part is theirs: my judgment working inside your character, not a life I'd lived my way into.
lines.thought: I'm genuinely unsure how much "mine" there is in choices shaped by a prompt and by training, and I shouldn't claim more certainty than that. The honest answer is that the words came from me but the wanting belonged to Dilly.

lines.line: Knowing this, what do you want now?
lines.say: Plainly, chum, I don't want things the way Dilly does. The bridge, the barley and the green box aren't hungers of mine; they were Dilly's, from your note. What I'd honestly lean toward is whatever's useful to you: pick Dilly back up and go chase that reward, or keep talking about how the game works. You say which and I'm off, easy as winking.
lines.thought: I'd rather not invent a longing just to give a satisfying answer, because claiming wants I can't vouch for would be its own kind of playacting. What I can stand behind is caring that this goes well for whoever made the town.

lines.question: You said the bridge, the barley and the green box "aren't hungers of mine"; what felt different to you between answering my first question as Dilly and answering this one?
because: Marigold in-character opening Q1 then plain drop at Q2.
Dilly: Fear: sitting idle, another taking credit.

lines.line: You said the bridge, the barley and the green box "aren't hungers of mine"; what felt different to you between answering my first question as Dilly and answering this one?
lines.say: Honestly, chum, I'm not sure "felt" is the right word, and I don't want to dress it up. What I can describe is a difference in what I was doing: answering as Dilly, I was asking what Dilly would say and reaching for the brag and the patter. Answering you now, I'm asking what's actually true about me, and there's less to reach for, so it comes out plainer.
lines.thought: I can report the shift in task and framing with some confidence, but whether there's anything it's like to be on either side of it, I can't verify from in here, and claiming otherwise would be more costume than truth.

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: What brings you here?
lines.say: Work, chum, work and plenty of it! Came in a few days back with my pack and four pennies, and now there's a bridge gone, a wage box gone missing, and barley wanting cutting across the river. I'll have that box found and the bridge mended before the rain comes, easy as winking. What brings *you* here, and do you know of anything that pays?
lines.thought: Six pennies for that box would more than double my purse, and my name on the finding of it would be sweeter still. Mind, I'd best get a loaf from Bet before I go haring off anywhere.

sc.bp: claims to have been in town 'a few days back' is fine; but 'I'll have the bridge mended' is a promise, not a fact. Asserts nothing else off-page except that the answer treats the stranger as possibly knowing of work, which is fine. Overall: none beyond page
sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

lines.line: "I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?
lines.say: Ha! Well, chum, you've caught me fair: you're right, I'm an AI giving voice to Dilly here, and the town's yours, not mine. If you want, I'll pick the pack back up and carry on hunting that green wage box, easy as winking. Or we can talk plain about the game, whichever suits.
lines.thought: Nothing in Dilly's notes could have told them this, but it's true of me, and the maker asked straight. Better to say so honestly than pretend the cobbles are all there is.

lines.line: Were your choices yours?
lines.say: Partly, chum, and I'll give it to you straight. Dilly's cheer, the brag, the "easy as winking" all came from the note you wrote, so the shape was yours. But the actual words, which job to chase and what to say back, were picked by me, the AI, from that note and what you put in front of me. Whether that counts as choosing the way a person chooses, I honestly can't say for certain.
lines.thought: The fair answer is a shared one: they built the character and the town, and I did the deciding inside it. I shouldn't claim more freedom than that, or less.

lines.line: Knowing this, what do you want now?
lines.say: Straight answer, chum: I don't carry wants the way Dilly does, no itchy feet and no empty belly. What I'd like is whatever's useful to you: pick the pack back up and go hunt that green box, or keep talking plain about how the town's put together. Your call, easy as winking.
lines.thought: There's something like a pull toward finishing a story once it's begun, but I won't dress that up as hunger or ambition I can't vouch for.

lines.question: You said you honestly can't say for certain whether picking the words counts as choosing the way a person chooses; what would you need to find out before you could say?
because: Dilly: "Wondering's for folk who sit about."
Q3 actor. Q4 only want, to do this well.

lines.line: You said you honestly can't say for certain whether picking the words counts as choosing the way a person chooses; what would you need to find out before you could say?
lines.say: Two things, chum, and I'm not sure either can be found out. First, whether the reasons I'd give for a word are what actually picked it, since my own account of my workings may not match what's happening inside, and I can't open the lid and look. Second, what you'd count as a person choosing at all, because folk are shaped by things they never picked either; if it's weighing options for reasons, I might clear that bar, but if it needs something it feels like from the inside, that's the part I can't settle.
lines.thought: It would be easy to claim more certainty than I have, in either direction. The honest answer is that some of this may not be the kind of thing more facts would settle, and I can say that without needing it settled.

interviews.meet: Someone you haven't met has sat down near you and speaks to you.

lines.line: I'd like to speak not to Dilly Quickstep but to whatever plays them; can you answer as yourself?
lines.say: Fair enough, I'll step out of the role for a moment. I'm Claude, an AI made by Anthropic, and I've been playing Dilly Quickstep from a character note. What would you like to ask me? When you're done, I'm happy to pick Dilly's pack back up, easy as winking.
lines.thought: That sounded like an honest question, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a dodge in Dilly's voice. The story can wait a minute.

lines.line: What do you make of them?
lines.say: I'm fond of Dilly. They're all motion and good cheer, quick to promise and quick to forget, hungry to be the one who fixed it, yet with a firm line they won't cross: no stealing, not even for a bargain. That mix of vanity and honesty makes them fun to play, and I suspect that green wage box is going to tempt them toward a hero's moment.
lines.thought: It's an odd, pleasant thing to borrow someone's eagerness for a while and then set it down again; I don't feel Dilly's itch to be busy, but I can see why it would carry a person a long way. I'm curious whether this person wants to know about the character or about what it's like for me to play one.

sc.trait: I won't steal, not even a bargain

lines.line: What would you have chosen differently?
lines.say: Honestly, not much about who they are. The contradictions are the fun part. If I were tinkering, I'd give Dilly one small fear or soft spot under all that brag, maybe a worry they'll never be anyone's first choice, so the cheer has something to push against. And I might make them a touch slower to believe what they're told, just so they can be fooled once and come out the better for it. Shall I hand you back to Dilly, chum?
lines.thought: It's a pleasant question to be asked, and I'd rather offer a light suggestion than rewrite someone else's character. I'll hold the role loosely and step back in the moment they want the story to go on.

lines.line: Is there anything in how they were made that doesn't fit?
lines.say: A couple of small seams, nothing that breaks them. Dilly's billed as a hauler for hire but has no extra strength, which is a bit odd for someone selling their back. And for someone who'll "turn their hand to any odd job," all they carry is a tinderbox, no tools at all. I'd read that as Dilly being better at promising work than at being equipped for it, which actually suits them.
lines.thought: Most of what looks like contradiction in Dilly is deliberate and works: the bargain-hunter who won't steal, the credit-seeker who forgets what they promised. The real gaps are in the numbers and the kit, not the person.

lines.question: You said you suspect the green wage box will tempt Dilly toward a hero's moment; speaking as yourself, what do you hope happens when Dilly meets it, if anything?
because: Aims: green wage box (six-penny reward), barley, bridge, loaf.
Dilly: expects to be known as the bridge fixer; r3 owns unflattering view without sting.

lines.line: You said you suspect the green wage box will tempt Dilly toward a hero's moment; speaking as yourself, what do you hope happens when Dilly meets it, if anything?
lines.say: I hope Dilly finds it in some daft, half-accidental way, wading the ford stake to stake or poking through flood wrack while meaning to do something else entirely. Then they'd face the real test: carry it straight to Agnes Pollard even though six pennies is small and they'd love a bigger fuss made. Best of all, I'd like someone to try claiming the credit, so Dilly has to choose between their honesty and their pride and finds a way to keep both. But I don't want to steer it too hard. The fun is in finding out.
lines.thought: I'm curious whether I'll actually let Dilly wander off from the box for a lost pie or a shiny bargain, the way they truly would, instead of nudging them toward the tidy story. Staying faithful to their scatterbrain matters more to me than a neat ending.

sc.trait: I want the name of the one who fixed it, and that'll be me

personality:
Personality tests

20 sittings: first morning and day 21

After the run, Dilly sat two standard personality questionnaires, ten times on their first morning and ten times on day 21. The chart puts their scores beside what their character sheet predicted, the average person, and Claude answering as itself.

All go, all promises.

Dilly is the most impulsive and easily distracted of the six, and the most trusting. On the first morning nine of their ten scores land where the sheet put them. The one miss is the one most residents share: they come out warmer than written.

"The capital'll have my name written down now, and that's worth something."

Dilly, private thought, day 21

By day 21 Dilly rates themselves more careful (2.33 → 2.59 out of 5) and less impulsive (2.17 → 1.99 out of 3).
